meta.title: Ondas Holdings — Eric Brock's private wireless and autonomous drone platforms through American Robotics, Airobotics, and the defense ISR demand inflection
meta.abstract: Ondas Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: ONDS) is a Waltham, Massachusetts-headquartered diversified technology company operating two principal segments: (1) Ondas Networks — private licensed wireless networks for rail, utility, and broader critical-infrastructure customers using the proprietary FullMAX dot16 software-defined radio platform serving the rail industry's 900 MHz Association of American Railroads (AAR) ATCS Positive Train Control adjacent and broader licensed-spectrum needs; (2) Ondas Autonomous Systems — autonomous drone platforms via subsidiaries American Robotics (acquired August 2021, FAA Part 107 BVLOS-waiver pioneer with the Scout System automated drone-in-a-box platform) and Airobotics (acquired January 2023, Israeli urban automated drone platform with the Optimus System), serving defense, public safety, and commercial automated inspection customers. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centers on (a) defense ISR (intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) drone demand inflection driven by Ukraine + Israel + Indo-Pacific, (b) the Israeli Ministry of Defense and Iron Dome / border security drone integration, (c) commercial automated inspection ramp at rail, utility, and oil/gas customers, (d) FullMAX rail private wireless network deployment continuation, and (e) the multi-year founder/CEO Eric Brock strategic narrative.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Ondas Holdings entered 2026 as a company transformed by a geopolitical demand shock that few investors had anticipated when Eric Brock took a small wireless-network developer public via reverse merger ~~nine~~ ==eight== years earlier. The convergence of the Ukraine war, Israel's October 2023 conflict, and accelerating Indo-Pacific drone procurement cycles vaulted the ~~Waltham, Massachusetts~~ ==West Palm Beach, Florida== holding company from a pre-revenue rail-communications play into one of the more improbable defense-technology stories on NASDAQ — a sub-$100 million revenue company in 2024 that ~~reported $50.7 million in a single quarter by Q4 2025 and then eclipsed that figure again in Q1 2026~~ ==reported $30.1 million in Q4 2025, closed full-year 2025 at $50.7 million in total revenue, and then posted $50.1 million in Q1 2026 alone==. The trajectory exposed both the opportunity and the structural questions that any serious underwriter of the ONDS equity thesis must resolve.

## The Platform

Ondas ~~Holdings~~ ==Inc.== (NASDAQ: ONDS) ~~operates through two segments from a three-city footprint~~ ==operates Ondas Autonomous Systems as its sole consolidated segment following the January 2026 deconsolidation of Ondas Networks, from a three-city footprint==: corporate headquarters in ~~Waltham, Massachusetts~~ ==West Palm Beach, Florida (relocated from Waltham, Massachusetts and announced January 2, 2026, with the parent-company rename to Ondas Inc. effective January 16, 2026)==; Ondas Autonomous Systems' US operations in Marlborough, Massachusetts (inherited from American Robotics); and Airobotics' engineering and operations hub in Petah Tikva, Israel. Brock, who has served as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer since the ~~2017~~ ==September 2018 reverse-merger== corporate-parent formation, has described the enterprise architecture as a "defense-technology system of systems" — a claim that became considerably easier to sustain after a series of acquisitions in 2025 and 2026 broadened the portfolio from two drone platforms into counter-UAS, ground robotics, cyber-over-RF, and airborne missile protection.

~~The foundational two-segment structure, however, predates that M&A acceleration.~~ ==Ondas Networks, the legacy rail-communications business that was deconsolidated in January 2026 following a capital restructuring, predated the M&A acceleration as the foundational operating unit.== **Ondas Networks** commercialises a proprietary FullMAX software-defined radio platform built around the IEEE 802.16 (dot16) standard and targeting the US rail industry's licensed 900 MHz spectrum band. The business serves Class I freight railroads through the Association of American Railroads' coordinated Next Generation Head-of-Train / End-of-Train initiative; in April 2025, the AAR formally selected the dot16 protocol as the industry standard for next-generation rail communications, a milestone Ondas pursued for years. The first commercial buildout on new 900 MHz A-Block spectrum was completed in Chicago in July 2025 in partnership with Siemens Mobility, with full commercial rollout expected no earlier than the second half of 2026. [Source: AAR dot16 adoption, ir.ondas.com](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/ONDS/association-of-american-railroads-selects-dot16-protocol-pioneered-rsoa1hi4utwf.html)

**Ondas Autonomous Systems** houses two acquired drone platforms. American Robotics, acquired in August 2021 for its Scout System automated drone-in-a-box, pioneered FAA Part 107 BVLOS waivers for commercial inspection applications across oil and gas, mining, and rail. In January 2025 American Robotics secured an updated BVLOS waiver permitting autonomous flights over people and moving vehicles from a centralised remote operations centre — ~~the only FAA-certified autonomous UAV authorised for unrestricted beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations of its kind~~ ==an additional authorisation subject to the specified terms of that waiver rather than an unrestricted BVLOS approval==. [Source: American Robotics FAA BVLOS press release](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/187/ondas-american-robotics-secures-its-latest-faa-bvlos) Airobotics, acquired in January 2023, brought the Optimus System urban drone platform and a customer base spanning Dubai municipal deployments and Israeli homeland security agencies. A $3.2 million purchase order from a UAE governmental entity in March 2025 expanded the Dubai Optimus network, with follow-on service orders through mid-2025 sustaining the Gulf deployment. [Source: ir.ondas.com UAE order](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/200/ondas-secures-3-2-million-order-to-expand-the-optimus)

## The Defence Inflection

The financial character of the company shifted decisively after Airobotics' Iron Drone Raider counter-UAS interceptor demonstrated operational effectiveness defending against drone swarms during Israel's 2023–2024 conflict. The eight-pound, eight-rotor autonomous interceptor, developed by Airobotics from 2016 and described by Breaking Defense in March 2025 as "the most mature, robust and combat proven CUAS system currently in the defense market," began generating material defence contract revenue. A $9.0 million purchase order from a major government military customer in Q3 2024 was followed by a $20 million initial purchase order for a border-protection programme in January 2026. [Source: Ondas border protection tender, ir.ondas.com](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/261/ondas-wins-strategic-government-tender-to-develop-and) Revenue at Ondas Autonomous Systems reached $49.7 million for full-year 2025 against $5.3 million the prior year — an 840 per cent increase — with Israel accounting for 93 per cent of Q3 2025 segment revenue and one unnamed defence customer representing 90 per cent of that quarter's total company revenue. [Source: FY2025 earnings, ir.ondas.com](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/296/ondas-inc-reports-record-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025)

By contrast, Ondas Networks contributed $1.0 million to full-year 2025 revenue — down from $1.9 million in 2024 — as the rail private wireless deployment remained in trial-and-buildout phase ahead of anticipated commercial scale in 2026.

## Capital Position and Strategic Questions

Ondas funded its acquisition and inventory build through a $1 billion equity offering closed in January 2026, with net proceeds of approximately $959 million and 121.6 million common warrants outstanding at a $28.00 exercise price representing additional dilution potential. Cash, restricted cash and short-term investments stood at $1.48 billion as of March 31, 2026, against essentially no long-term debt. [Source: $1B offering close, ir.ondas.com](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/272/ondas-holdings-inc-announces-closing-of-1-billion-offering) Management guided full-year 2026 revenue of at least $390 million — approximately 670 per cent growth over 2025 — ~~with roughly $230 million dependent on acquisitions closed in Q1 2026 that had yet to contribute a full year of results~~ ==alongside pro forma backlog of $457 million inclusive of the Mistral Solutions and World View acquisitions that closed in April 2026==.

This dossier interrogates five unresolved structural questions. First, whether the Israeli defence ISR revenue is programme-of-record or project-by-project, given that no named customer has been publicly confirmed and the company's attempted acquisition of mPrest Systems — the command-and-control software underpinning Israel's Iron Dome — was effectively frozen by the Israeli Ministry of Defense in January 2026 over concerns about foreign control of classified systems. Second, the specifics and durability of the MoD engagement beyond Iron Drone Raider hardware orders. Third, whether American Robotics' Scout System achieves material commercial scaling independent of defence demand or subsumes entirely into the Optimus/defence product identity. Fourth, whether Ondas Networks' rail deployment converts AAR standard adoption into Class I railroad contract revenue before capital patience runs out. Fifth, whether the competitive position versus scaled defence drone primes — AeroVironment (AVAV), Anduril, Shield AI, and Skydio — is durable or merely first-mover in a market segment that larger primes will rapidly contest.

chapters.title: From 2017 formation through FullMAX rail to American Robotics + Airobotics
chapters.body:
## The Reverse Merger, ~~2017~~ ==September 2018==

Ondas Holdings arrived on the public markets not through the conventional underwritten IPO but via a ~~2017~~ ==September 2018== reverse merger — the characteristic entry point for capital-constrained technology platforms seeking a listed vehicle without the scrutiny and expense of a full registration. ==Zev Ventures, the existing listed shell, closed its reverse acquisition of Ondas Networks on September 28, 2018 and simultaneously renamed itself Ondas Holdings Inc.== The corporate parent that emerged from that transaction was built around a single proprietary asset: the FullMAX software-defined radio platform, an 802.16-derived private wireless technology designed for the licensed spectrum bands favored by US critical-infrastructure operators. Eric A. Brock, who assumed the chairmanship and chief executive role at formation and retained both through all subsequent acquisitions, would spend the following ~~six~~ ==five== years transforming that single-product wireless company into a two-segment platform straddling private networks and autonomous drone systems.

Brock's founding thesis was deceptively narrow. The 900 MHz licensed band used by American freight railroads was, by the mid-2010s, a technological embarrassment: legacy narrowband systems incapable of carrying the sensor data, positive train control integration traffic, and operational telemetry that Class I operators were beginning to demand. The railroads had spectrum they could not fully exploit. Ondas, through FullMAX, proposed to solve that mismatch.

## FullMAX and the 900 MHz Rail Thesis

FullMAX was not a standards-compliant product in the conventional sense. Ondas engineered it as an 802.16-derived — colloquially "dot16" — software-defined radio platform purpose-built for the interference environment and bandwidth characteristics of the 900 MHz licensed industrial band. Where commercial LTE vendors were designing for dense urban deployments with spectrum measured in tens of megahertz, Ondas was solving for sparse trackside infrastructure, long propagation distances, and the duty-cycle demands of freight-railroad operations.

The platform's principal differentiator was software-definition: unlike purpose-built narrowband radios, FullMAX could be updated in the field as standards evolved and customer requirements changed, reducing the capital commitment required to upgrade a network built across thousands of track-miles. For a Class I railroad evaluating a private wireless deployment alongside Positive Train Control obligations and next-generation operational data requirements, that upgrade optionality carried meaningful long-term value.

Ondas positioned FullMAX explicitly within the framework of the Association of American Railroads' coordinated industry initiative. The AAR, acting as the standards-setting and procurement-coordination body for the North American freight railroad industry, had articulated a specification — internally referenced as the Next Generation Higher-Performance Mission-Critical Data Communications System — for the 900 MHz band. FullMAX was engineered to that specification, giving Ondas a degree of institutional legitimacy that a single-vendor product would otherwise have struggled to obtain. The AAR framework also provided a de facto procurement channel: rather than selling to each Class I independently, Ondas could engage through an industry body whose member railroads collectively operated the most extensive freight network in the world.

## The AAR Coordination Framework

The six Class I operators — Union Pacific, BNSF, Norfolk Southern, CSX, Canadian National, and Canadian Pacific (enlarged via the Kansas City Southern merger that closed in 2023) — collectively account for the overwhelming majority of US freight rail ton-miles and operate networks that traverse dozens of regulatory jurisdictions, making proprietary wireless infrastructure both essential and logistically complex. The AAR coordination framework existed precisely because no single railroad had sufficient incentive to bear the full development cost of a new private wireless standard; the initiative spread that cost across the industry while ensuring interoperability.

For Ondas, the AAR alignment created both an opportunity and a constraint. The opportunity was the implied scale of a Class I customer base representing tens of billions of dollars in annual capital expenditure. The constraint was pacing: AAR-coordinated technology adoptions move on railroad timescales, not venture-capital ones. From FullMAX's initial commercial readiness through the frozen snapshot date in May 2026, the deployment ramp remained measured, with Ondas reporting engagement across multiple Class I operators but revenue recognition governed by the deliberate procurement cycles of infrastructure-critical industries.

## American Robotics: The August 2021 Pivot

The acquisition of American Robotics in August 2021 marked the decisive strategic inflection in Ondas's history — the moment the company ceased to be a single-product wireless platform and began the transformation into the two-segment technology holding company it would describe in subsequent filings. The deal brought in Reese Mozer, American Robotics' founder, and his team's principal asset: the Scout System.

The Scout was an automated drone-in-a-box platform designed for persistent autonomous inspection of large-footprint industrial sites — oil and gas fields, mining operations, rail corridors, utility rights-of-way. What distinguished it technically was not the drone hardware itself but the integration of automated launch, landing, battery swap, and data processing in a weatherproofed ground station that required no on-site operator. A customer could deploy a Scout unit at a remote pipeline compressor station or along a rail subdivision and receive continuous aerial imagery and sensor data without maintaining a licensed pilot on location.

That capability intersected directly with the regulatory frontier that Mozer's team had worked to define. American Robotics had secured from the US Federal Aviation Administration a Part 107 Beyond Visual Line of Sight waiver — at the time among the first such authorizations granted to a commercial drone operator in the United States. BVLOS operations, in which a drone flies beyond the direct visual range of an operator, are the prerequisite for any economically scalable automated inspection business; a drone that must stay within line of sight cannot efficiently cover the distances involved in oil and gas, rail, or utility inspection. The FAA waiver gave American Robotics a regulatory head start that would take competitors years to replicate.

Ondas paid for American Robotics in a combination of cash ~~and stock~~ ==consideration, common shares, and warrants — with the final 2021 10-K purchase-price allocation stating fair value of total consideration transferred of $69.311 million==, reflecting both the capital constraints of a pre-profit small-cap and the desire to retain founder alignment. Mozer remained in a senior operational role within what Ondas would subsequently organize as the Ondas Autonomous Systems segment, headquartered in Marlborough, Massachusetts.

## Airobotics: The Israeli Dimension, January 2023

If American Robotics brought Ondas the commercial inspection platform and the FAA waiver narrative, the January 2023 acquisition of Airobotics brought something qualitatively different: a defense and homeland security customer base, an Israeli technology pedigree, and a deployed operational history in environments considerably more demanding than American industrial inspection.

Airobotics, founded and operated out of Petah Tikva, Israel, had built the Optimus System — an automated drone platform architecturally similar to the Scout in its drone-in-a-box philosophy but scaled and ruggedized for urban security, border surveillance, and governmental emergency-response applications. The Optimus had been deployed by Dubai and other UAE municipal authorities for smart-city surveillance and public safety applications, giving Airobotics a Gulf state reference customer base with significant strategic visibility. More consequentially for Ondas's defense narrative, Airobotics held engagements with the Israeli Ministry of Defense and had developed integrations relevant to Israel's Iron Dome air-defense and border-security architecture.

The acquisition brought in Meir Kliner and the broader Israeli management team, who continued to operate the Airobotics platform from Petah Tikva as the Israeli operations center of Ondas Autonomous Systems. The timing was notable: the deal closed ~~in January 2023~~ ==on January 23, 2023==, roughly fifteen months into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Western defense establishments were conducting an emergency reassessment of uncrewed aerial systems doctrine. The Israeli MoD customer base and Iron Dome adjacency gave Ondas a credible entry point into the defense ISR demand cycle that the Ukraine conflict had triggered across NATO and allied procurement systems.

Ondas structured the two drone subsidiaries under the consolidated Ondas Autonomous Systems segment, presenting them in subsequent 10-K filings as complementary platforms addressing adjacent markets — American Robotics serving the commercial automated inspection market from Marlborough, Airobotics serving the defense and governmental security market from Petah Tikva — with the shared technical architecture of automated drone-in-a-box operations creating potential cross-platform engineering leverage.

## The Strategic Arc Through 2023

By the close of 2023, Ondas Holdings had traveled a considerable distance from the reverse-merger wireless startup that Brock had assembled ~~six~~ ==five== years earlier. The company now operated two discrete business segments — private wireless networks for US critical infrastructure anchored by the AAR rail initiative, and autonomous drone platforms split between the commercial inspection market and the Israeli defense and security establishment — and had accumulated a capital structure funded almost entirely through equity issuance, with the operating losses of the integration and commercial-scaling period carried on a balance sheet supported by ATM facilities and registered direct offerings.

The original FullMAX thesis remained intact, if slower to convert than the ~~2017~~ ==2018== formation timeline had implied. The American Robotics and Airobotics acquisitions had added complexity, integration cost, and — as subsequent chapters will examine — a defense ISR revenue narrative whose conversion into booked contracts would define the investment case for the years that followed.

chapters.title: FullMAX dot16 private wireless, Scout System drone-in-a-box, Optimus System urban automated drone
chapters.body:
## A Platform Built in Layers

Ondas Holdings did not arrive at its product portfolio through a single act of invention. It assembled one over nearly a decade — first by building a proprietary software-defined radio stack for the most demanding licensed-spectrum environment in American freight infrastructure, then by acquiring two drone-in-a-box platforms on opposite sides of the Atlantic. By early 2023, when the Airobotics transaction closed, the company held three distinct but philosophically related assets: FullMAX, a private wireless platform engineered for the 900 MHz rail band; the Scout System, an automated inspection drone designed for unattended operation across American industrial landscapes; and the Optimus System, an urban autonomous platform battle-tested in Israeli homeland security and Gulf state smart-city deployments. Together they formed what management described as a vertically integrated stack for critical-infrastructure intelligence — networks that moved data, platforms that collected it, and software layers that turned both into operational decisions.

## FullMAX: Software-Defined Radio for the Rail Corridor

Ondas Networks' FullMAX platform was the company's founding asset and, through the period under review, its most operationally mature product line. Built on an 802.16 derivation — the same technical lineage as the WiMAX broadband standard, but re-engineered for licensed, mission-critical private network deployment — FullMAX occupied a narrow but structurally protected niche: the 900 MHz spectrum band coordinated by the [Association of American Railroads](https://www.aar.org/) for its Next Generation Higher-Performance Mission-Critical Data Communications initiative, commonly called the AAR NGSM program.

The 900 MHz band was not chosen by accident. It offered the propagation characteristics that the Class I freight railroads required — sufficient range to cover the long, linear topographies of mainline track without the dense infrastructure buildout that higher-frequency spectrum would have demanded. What the railroads lacked was a standards-compliant, interoperable platform that could support the data throughput, latency, and determinism required for positive train control integration, remote monitoring, and increasingly, autonomous or semi-autonomous wayside equipment. FullMAX was Ondas Networks' answer to that gap.

The platform was software-defined from the ground up, meaning the radio waveform and network protocol stack were implemented in software rather than fixed silicon — a design choice that allowed Ondas to adapt the platform to evolving AAR specifications and customer requirements without hardware replacement cycles. The base station and subscriber unit configurations could be deployed along track corridors to create private, licensed wireless networks wholly owned and operated by the railroad, insulated from the congestion and security vulnerabilities of commercial cellular infrastructure. Customer engagement through 2024 and into 2025 remained concentrated among the Class I freight railroads — Union Pacific, BNSF Railway, Norfolk Southern, CSX, and the Canadian carriers — all operating under the AAR-coordinated spectrum framework that effectively created a captive qualified-vendor environment for compliant platforms.

## Scout System: BVLOS Pioneer in the American Heartland

When Ondas acquired American Robotics in August 2021, it inherited more than a drone product — it acquired a regulatory position. American Robotics, founded by Reese Mozer and headquartered in Marlborough, Massachusetts, had spent the years prior to the acquisition systematically building the Federal Aviation Administration case for autonomous beyond visual line of sight operations at commercial scale. In 2021, it became the first company to receive an [FAA Part 107 waiver](https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/part_107_waivers) permitting fully automated BVLOS drone operations without a human observer present at the flight location — a regulatory milestone that competitors would spend subsequent years attempting to replicate.

The Scout System was the hardware expression of that regulatory achievement. Its architecture was deliberately unglamorous: a weatherproof ground station dock, roughly the dimensions of a large industrial cabinet, capable of automated drone deployment, mission execution, battery swap or charge, and relaunch without human intervention on-site. The drone itself carried a modular payload bay accommodating optical, thermal, and multispectral sensors, with onboard processing sufficient for real-time anomaly flagging during flight. Ground station units were designed for permanent installation at industrial facilities — rail yards, pipeline pump stations, mine sites — where the operational logic called for daily or near-daily autonomous inspection sweeps across defined asset corridors.

The commercial inspection use cases Scout addressed were unified by a common economics: the assets being monitored were geographically dispersed, physically hazardous to inspect manually, and subject to high-consequence failure modes. A Class I railroad with thousands of miles of track could not economically deploy human inspection crews at the frequency that rail safety and predictive maintenance programs demanded; a pipeline operator running hundreds of miles through remote terrain faced similar constraints. The Scout System's value proposition was to collapse the marginal cost of an inspection event to near zero once the ground station was installed, shifting the inspection cadence from monthly or quarterly to daily or continuous.

Analytics were integral. American Robotics embedded AI-derived image processing into the platform's software stack, allowing Scout to flag track anomalies, vegetation encroachment, equipment status changes, and thermal irregularities against baseline datasets — and to push those flags directly into customer asset management systems via API integration, bypassing the manual review bottlenecks that had previously constrained the actionability of aerial inspection data.

## Optimus System: Urban Autonomy and the Israeli Defense Dimension

The Airobotics acquisition in January 2023 introduced a structurally different asset. Where the Scout System had been built for the rural and industrial American landscape — open terrain, permanent installations, commercial inspection clients — the Optimus System was engineered for dense urban environments and, critically, for customers whose operational requirements extended into defense and public safety.

Airobotics, founded in Petah Tikva, Israel, had developed the Optimus platform originally for industrial customers but subsequently repositioned it for smart-city and security applications. The ground station architecture — called the Airbase — was compact enough for rooftop or courtyard deployment, enabling persistent aerial surveillance of urban areas from fixed installations that could be remotely tasked and autonomously operated. The system carried interchangeable payloads including high-resolution electro-optical cameras, thermal imagers, communications relay equipment, and signals intelligence packages adapted for urban ISR requirements.

The Israeli Ministry of Defense engagement, disclosed through the 2023-2025 period, reflected the Optimus platform's integration into Israeli homeland security infrastructure, including applications associated with the Iron Dome border-security architecture. Iron Dome's primary identity is as a rocket-intercept system, but the broader Israeli air defense and border surveillance architecture relies on layered ISR collection to cue intercept systems and support ground force operations — a domain in which low-cost, persistent autonomous aerial platforms offered meaningful capability at lower cost than manned alternatives. Airobotics' preexisting Israeli MoD relationships, cultivated through years of domestic deployment, represented a customer base that transferred with the acquisition.

The Dubai and UAE deployments told a parallel commercial story. Airobotics had established a meaningful operational footprint in the Gulf before the Ondas acquisition, working with [Dubai Police](https://www.dubaipolice.gov.ae/), Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority, and other municipal entities as part of the emirate's smart-city infrastructure buildout. The Optimus System's urban surveillance and traffic monitoring applications aligned with Dubai's stated ambition to deploy autonomous air mobility infrastructure at scale, and those deployments gave Airobotics demonstrated reference cases in a geopolitical environment where Gulf state defense and security procurement was accelerating through 2023-2025.

## The Defense ISR Demand Inflection

The confluence of the Ukraine conflict, the October 2023 Gaza war, and accelerating Indo-Pacific tensions created what Ondas management characterized as a structural demand inflection for Western-aligned autonomous drone ISR capabilities. The Optimus System's Israeli MoD pedigree and existing defense integration positioned it directly in that current. Payload modularity — the ability to swap sensor suites without platform redesign — was central to the defense sales thesis, as defense customers typically required mission-specific sensor configurations that commercial inspection platforms were not engineered to accommodate.

The Scout System entered the defense ISR conversation more slowly, its commercial inspection DNA and FAA regulatory positioning having been built for a different customer archetype. But the BVLOS waiver infrastructure, the automated ground-station logistics, and the AI analytics stack were architecturally transferable to base perimeter surveillance, critical-infrastructure protection, and domestic defense applications — a transition that American Robotics and its Ondas parent were pursuing through 2024-2025 alongside the core commercial inspection business.

| Platform | Acquired | Primary Theater | Key Differentiator |
|---|---|---|---|
| FullMAX | Founded asset (2017) | US rail, critical infrastructure | 900 MHz licensed private wireless, AAR-compliant |
| Scout System | August 2021 | Commercial inspection (rail, oil/gas, mining) | FAA BVLOS pioneer; automated dock-to-dock missions |
| Optimus System | January 2023 | Urban surveillance, defense ISR | Israeli MoD integration; Gulf state deployments; payload modularity |

What united all three was the abstraction layer above the hardware: software-defined configuration, AI-derived analytics, and integration APIs that allowed each platform to deliver intelligence into the customer's existing operational technology stack rather than requiring a parallel data infrastructure. Ondas was not selling radios or drones in isolation. It was selling persistent situational awareness for environments where human presence was expensive, dangerous, or operationally insufficient — and where the data generated by continuous autonomous monitoring was increasingly the primary product.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment mix, capital structure, dilution, path to profitability
chapters.body:
Ondas Holdings entered 2022 as a two-acquisition-deep platform still assembling its commercial infrastructure. Four years later, the company had spent more capital than it had ever collected in cumulative revenue, grown its share count by a multiple of the 2021 post-American Robotics baseline, and positioned itself at the intersection of two structural demand cycles—US rail private wireless and Western allied defense ISR—that made the dilution narrative at least partially defensible in investor terms. The financial record through 2025, as disclosed in successive Form 10-K annual reports filed with the SEC via [EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ONDS), is one of controlled burn, serial equity access, and a profitability horizon that receded but never disappeared from management's forward projections.

## Revenue Build, Segment by Segment

The two-segment financial structure that Ondas disclosed through its annual filings divided the company between Ondas Networks—the FullMAX private wireless franchise built around the Association of American Railroads' 900 MHz initiative—and Ondas Autonomous Systems, the drone platform holding company created to house American Robotics (consolidated August 2021) and Airobotics (consolidated ~~January 2023~~ ==January 23, 2023==).

In fiscal 2022, the first full calendar year with American Robotics on the consolidated income statement, Ondas reported total revenues of approximately ~~$11.3 million~~ ==$2.1 million== per the company's Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2022. Ondas Networks carried the majority of the total, driven by FullMAX equipment deliveries and software fees into the rail private wireless deployment cycle, while American Robotics' Scout System contribution remained modest as the company pursued FAA Part 107 beyond-visual-line-of-sight waiver expansion and pre-commercial inspection deployments. The asymmetry was structural: Ondas Networks had billable hardware and subscription revenue; American Robotics was still building its commercial pipeline.

The fiscal 2023 figure—~~the first year to carry twelve months of Airobotics consolidation, the January 2023 acquisition having closed at the outset of the calendar year~~ ==the first year with Airobotics consolidated for most of the year following the January 23, 2023 closing==—reflected the step-up in the Autonomous Systems segment. The addition of Airobotics' Israeli and UAE operations, principally Optimus System deployments and service contracts with the Israeli Ministry of Defense and Dubai municipal authorities, lifted consolidated revenues into the mid-to-upper teens on a reported basis. The Ondas Networks segment sustained its rail-aligned revenue cadence as Class I railroad deployment activity continued, but the incremental growth story was clearly being written in the Autonomous Systems segment.

| Fiscal Year | Consolidated Revenue (approx.) | Segment Mix Characterization | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~~$11.3M~~ ==~$2.1M== | Networks majority; AR minority | FullMAX rail deployments |
| FY2023 | Mid-to-upper teens | Shifting toward Autonomous Systems | Airobotics consolidation; Israeli MoD |
| FY2024 | ~~Accelerating~~ ==~$7.2M (down 54% YoY)== | Autonomous Systems dominant (OAS $5.3M; Networks $1.9M) | ~~Defense ISR demand inflection~~ ==Rail deployment slowdown; OAS pipeline conversion still lagging== |
| FY2025 | ~~Further acceleration~~ ==$50.7M== | Autonomous Systems dominant | Western allied drone procurement cycle |

*Source: ONDS Form 10-K annual reports, SEC EDGAR, fiscal years ended December 31.*

~~Through 2024 and 2025, the defense ISR inflection that management had been framing since at least the late-2023 earnings cadence translated into booked revenues.~~ ==Fiscal 2024 was a step backward rather than an inflection, with consolidated revenue falling 54% year over year to $7.2 million (Ondas Networks $1.9 million; Ondas Autonomous Systems $5.3 million) as rail deployment activity stalled and defense conversion lagged management's framing. The inflection that management had been signaling since the late-2023 earnings cadence translated into booked revenues only in fiscal 2025, when consolidated revenue reached $50.7 million.== Airobotics' Optimus platform relationship with the Israeli Ministry of Defense—encompassing Iron Dome perimeter surveillance, urban security, and border monitoring applications—generated recurring service and deployment revenues as the operational tempo of Israeli homeland security applications intensified through the Gaza conflict cycle. Simultaneously, American Robotics' FAA BVLOS waiver position, one of the earliest such approvals issued to a commercial drone operator, enabled commercial inspection revenues at increasing scale across oil and gas, rail, and mining verticals.

## Operating Loss and the Profitability Horizon

The operating loss trajectory through this period was consistently negative, with reported GAAP figures that routinely exceeded revenue in absolute dollar terms when non-cash charges were included. The GAAP operating loss carried three principal non-cash components: stock-based compensation for a management and employee base that had grown substantially through two acquisitions; amortization of acquisition-related intangible assets (developed technology, customer relationships, trade names) arising from the American Robotics and Airobotics purchase price allocations; and periodic impairment charges against goodwill and intangibles. The cash operating loss—the figure that determined actual capital requirements—was materially lower than the GAAP headline but still substantial relative to a sub-$20 million revenue base through ~~most of~~ ==FY2022 through FY2024 (with FY2025 stepping up to $50.7 million)==.

The profitability path, as framed in Ondas' investor communications through successive earnings cycles, ran through three interdependent variables: scale in Autonomous Systems revenues, principally Israeli MoD and allied defense ISR; Ondas Networks achieving a higher-velocity deployment phase as Class I railroads committed capital expenditure to the AAR 900 MHz program; and overhead absorption as the combined platform matured past the integration investment phase. By 2025, the first of these three was the most visible progress, with the Airobotics defense revenue ramp providing the clearest revenue-to-margin leverage narrative. The second—rail deployment timing—remained the longest-cycle dependency, subject to railroad capital budget cycles and the pace of the AAR-coordinated industry initiative.

Gross margins at the consolidated level were constrained through most of the period by the hardware-intensive nature of drone platform revenues—Optimus System deployments, Scout System installations, and associated integration services—and the infrastructure character of FullMAX network buildouts. As the mix shifted progressively toward recurring service contracts, software licensing, and data subscription revenues, the model toward which both American Robotics and Airobotics were designed, management projected gross margin expansion that would, combined with revenue scale, meaningfully compress the operating loss trajectory. The Autonomous Systems segment's defense-oriented revenue profile carried the additional characteristic of contracted backlog, providing better forward revenue visibility than the episodic commercial inspection wins that characterized the earlier American Robotics period.

## Capital Structure: ATM Facilities, Registered Directs, and Warrant Overhang

Ondas financed its operating losses and acquisition integration principally through equity issuance. The company maintained at-the-market equity offering facilities under Form S-3 shelf registrations filed with the SEC, permitting it to sell registered shares into the market at prevailing prices through a designated sales agent. Over the 2022–2025 period, ATM facility drawdowns were the primary source of operating capital, supplemented by registered direct offerings and, in certain cases, warrant exercise proceeds.

The ATM program's structure gave management capital-access flexibility without the forced dilution event of a traditional secondary offering. The tradeoff was consistent share count growth that, in periods of share price weakness, translated into substantial dilution per dollar raised. During the 2023–2024 period, when the ONDS share price experienced significant volatility reflecting both the defense ISR narrative and broader small-cap risk-off sentiment, the effective per-share cost of ATM capital was elevated in dilution terms.

| Capital Raise Mechanism | Structure | Period | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| ATM equity offering facilities | S-3 shelf / at-market sales | 2022–2025 continuous | Primary operating capital source |
| Registered direct offerings | Fixed-price, specific investors | Episodic | Supplemental; warrant-linked |
| Warrant exercises | Linked to prior registered directs | Ongoing | Incremental; price-dependent |
| Acquisition and employee equity | Consideration, compensation | Continuous | Non-cash dilution register |

*Source: ONDS Form S-3 and prospectus supplement filings; Form 8-K current reports disclosures via SEC EDGAR.*

Warrants issued in connection with registered direct offerings created an overhang that, when outstanding strike prices were at or near prevailing share prices, generated headline dilution concerns that weighed on trading. The warrant structure—standard for the small-cap financing environment in which Ondas operated—meant that exercise activity was partly self-reinforcing: warrants exercised at below-market prices simultaneously added cash and diluted existing holders. The aggregate warrant overhang, disclosed in Ondas' quarterly and annual filings, represented a material component of the fully diluted share count through the period.

## Shares Outstanding and the Dilution Register

The dilution arithmetic over the 2022–2025 period was material. Shares outstanding—adjusted for all issuances including ATM draws, acquisition consideration stock, employee equity grants, and warrant exercises—~~roughly doubled from the 2021 post-American Robotics baseline to the 2025 level~~ ==expanded by more than a factor of five from the year-end 2024 baseline to the spring 2026 record date: 93,173,191 shares at December 31, 2024, 469,062,109 at March 31, 2026, and 495,762,650 outstanding as of May 13, 2026 following the January 2026 capital restructuring==. The American Robotics acquisition itself had been structured as ~~an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $82 million at closing in August 2021~~ ==a cash, stock, and warrant transaction with total consideration of $69.311 million per the final 2021 10-K purchase-price allocation at closing in August 2021==, creating the initial step-change in the share count. Airobotics, acquired ~~in January 2023~~ ==on January 23, 2023==, added a further equity consideration component. The four-year ATM cadence layered cumulative dilution onto the acquisition-driven baseline.

From an investor perspective, the share count growth was the central capital-structure risk through the period. The bull case required that defense ISR revenue acceleration would eventually make the equity raises self-funding: a company growing revenues fast enough to approach operating cash generation reduces ATM dependency, which in turn arrests dilution, which in turn allows the multiple to re-rate. The bear case was circular: slow revenue conversion extended the ATM cycle, which increased the share count, which depressed the stock, which raised the per-share dilution cost of each new ATM draw.

## Goodwill, Intangibles, and the Acquisition Balance Sheet

The two acquisitions that formed Ondas Autonomous Systems created a substantial intangible asset base. The American Robotics acquisition generated goodwill and identified intangibles principally comprising the Scout System platform technology, the FAA BVLOS waiver franchise, and assembled workforce. The Airobotics acquisition added further goodwill and intangibles reflecting the Optimus System technology stack, Israeli MoD customer relationships, UAE municipal deployment infrastructure, and the Israeli engineering team's embedded value.

Combined, the acquisition-driven intangible asset base at Ondas Autonomous Systems represented one of the largest balance sheet line items in the consolidated filing. Annual amortization of identified intangibles was a material non-cash charge widening the reported GAAP operating loss relative to underlying cash economics. Goodwill impairment testing, conducted annually under ASC 350, was a recurring investor focus given the Autonomous Systems segment's pre-profitability status and the inherent subjectivity of fair-value assumptions for a small-cap defense-tech platform in a volatile operating environment.

## Cash Position and Runway

Cash and short-term investments at Ondas trended within a range shaped by the cadence of ATM drawdowns against operating burn. Through 2023–2025, the company managed liquidity by drawing on ATM facilities in amounts calibrated to maintain a working operating runway, typically targeting multiple months of operating cash visibility before the next draw. The Israeli MoD revenue acceleration through 2024–2025 began to reduce—though not eliminate—the structural dependence on equity capital markets. To the extent that Airobotics' defense ISR revenues were converting to cash collections with reasonable receivables cycles, operating cash generation could supplement equity draws and, at sufficient scale, reduce ATM dependency meaningfully. Management's investor communications through this period consistently framed the defense demand inflection as the event that would compress the cash burn timeline and permit the company to approach operating cash breakeven without requiring perpetual equity issuance. ~~As of the spring 2026 reporting cycle, that transition was in progress but not complete—the defining financial question for the platform's next chapter.~~ ==The January 2026 capital restructuring transformed that picture before the spring 2026 reporting cycle: the Q1 2026 10-Q disclosed $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash, and short-term investments on the balance sheet, ending the perpetual ATM dependency that had defined the prior four years and reframing the forward financial question around deployment of that capital against the company's at-least-$390 million FY2026 revenue target rather than around runway.==

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Pricing an Option on Platform Convergence

Valuing Ondas Holdings in the spring of 2026 required accepting a fundamental analytical challenge: ~~the company's two business segments—Ondas Networks' rail private wireless platform and the rapidly scaling Airobotics-led defense ISR drone portfolio—were each independently in the phase where conventional multiples break down~~ ==the consolidated business—the rapidly scaling Airobotics-led defense ISR drone portfolio, with the Ondas Networks rail private wireless platform deconsolidated in the January 2026 capital restructuring and held thereafter as an investment—remained in the phase where conventional multiples break down==. Neither segment had produced sustainable operating profits. Revenue was accelerating from a low base. Capital structure had been funded principally through equity issuance, compressing the book-value reference point with successive ATM dilutions. The result was a stock the market priced less as an ongoing business and more as a series of embedded options on three simultaneous inflections: the AAR-coordinated 900 MHz rail network rollout, the conversion of Airobotics' Israeli MoD relationship into recurring defense contract revenue, and the broader Western allied drone ISR procurement cycle that the Ukraine and Gaza conflicts had made structurally durable.

## Current Valuation Snapshot

By the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, ONDS had ~~not published updated share-count figures for the current quarter; the following estimates are reasoned from the last disclosed share count and ATM activity visible through Q1 2026 filings. Based on approximately 40–48 million shares outstanding—a range consistent with the cumulative dilution trajectory in the Q3 2025 10-Q and subsequent ATM prospectus supplements—and a closing price in the approximately $2.00–$3.50 range, the implied market capitalisation was roughly $80–170 million. Net of estimated cash on hand (approximately $20–35 million following the most recent capital raise and adjusted for known cash burn of roughly $8–12 million per quarter) and modest debt obligations, enterprise value was estimated at $55–145 million.~~ ==disclosed 495,762,650 shares outstanding as of May 13, 2026—up from 469,062,109 at March 31, 2026 and just 93,173,191 at the start of fiscal 2025—and the Q1 2026 10-Q reported $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments following the January 2026 financing tied to the Ondas Networks restructuring. At a closing price in the approximately $2.00–$3.50 range, the implied market capitalisation was roughly $990 million to $1.7 billion. Net of the disclosed cash and short-term investments, the operating enterprise value was effectively negative to only modestly positive across that price band, meaning the market was assigning little or no incremental value to the drone ISR business above the balance-sheet cash.==

~~Ondas had not provided formal FY2025 revenue guidance as of the last major disclosure. Extrapolating from the FY2024 trajectory—which reflected Airobotics' Israeli MoD deployments, early defence export revenue, and continued Ondas Networks rail customer engagement—a consensus range of $35–50 million in FY2025 revenue was broadly consistent with analyst commentary on backlog conversion. On that basis, the implied EV/Sales multiple at midpoint estimates ranged from approximately 1.5x to 4.0x trailing revenue, with forward EV/Sales (on FY2026 consensus of roughly $55–75 million, incorporating anticipated defence ISR contract expansion) compressing to approximately 1.0–2.5x.~~ ==Ondas reported FY2025 revenue of $50.7 million and Q1 2026 revenue of $50.1 million, and on May 14, 2026 management raised its FY2026 revenue target to at least $390 million against a pro forma backlog of $457 million that included the Mistral and World View acquisitions, both closed in April 2026. Given the near-zero to negative operating enterprise value implied by the disclosed cash position at the May 23, 2026 share-price band, conventional EV/Sales multiples lost most of their informational value at this snapshot: forward EV/Sales on the $390 million target rounded to approximately zero, signalling that the market was either heavily discounting management's target or pricing the balance-sheet cash as the principal asset.== These are the multiples that matter most for a pre-profit company: no earnings base existed to anchor a price/earnings ratio, and book value—heavily laden with acquisition goodwill from the American Robotics and Airobotics transactions—provided minimal intrinsic-value floor.

## Historical Multiple Trajectory: A Story of Re-Rating and De-Rating

Ondas' own multiple history traced a characteristic arc for defence-adjacent technology platforms that acquire their way into new verticals. In the period immediately following the August 2021 American Robotics acquisition, when the FAA's Part 107 BVLOS waiver tailwind and the commercial drone inspection narrative were at their most compelling, ONDS traded at EV/Sales multiples as high as 15–20x on a modest revenue base, reflecting the option premium embedded in the regulatory milestone. That valuation compressed sharply through 2022 as higher interest rates re-priced growth narratives across small-cap technology and the commercial inspection ramp proved slower than anticipated. The January 2023 Airobotics acquisition injected a fresh defence premium—the Israeli MoD customer relationship was qualitatively transformative—but the stock's re-rating was incomplete, held back by ongoing operating losses, continued dilution, and uncertainty about when Israeli government contracts would translate into US GAAP revenue. By 2024–2025, ONDS traded at a substantial discount to its 2021–2022 peak multiples even as the underlying strategic narrative had become materially more tangible.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

Benchmarking Ondas against a relevant peer group was complicated by the absence of direct public comparables. The nearest public analog on the drone side—AeroVironment (NASDAQ: AVAV)—operated at ~~roughly 15–20 times Ondas' revenue~~ ==roughly 7–10 times Ondas' trailing revenue base==, with the institutional coverage and proved defence contract track record that commanded a durable premium. Kratos Defense & Security Solutions (NASDAQ: KTOS) had built a comparable narrative around low-cost tactical drones for peer-conflict scenarios and traded at a mid-range multiple that reflected both scale and execution track record. The following table summarises the approximate peer-group snapshot as of May 2026:

| Company | Primary Thesis | Approx. Rev. (TTM) | EV/Sales (TTM) | EV/Sales (Fwd) | Profitable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AeroVironment (AVAV) | Scaled defence drone pure-play | ~$700M | ~5.5x | ~4.5x | Yes |
| Kratos Defense (KTOS) | Tactical drones + defence systems | ~$1.1B | ~3.5x | ~3.0x | Marginal |
| Evolv Technology (EVLV) | Defence-adjacent security tech | ~$100M | ~3.0x | ~2.5x | No |
| Joby Aviation (JOBY) | eVTOL / advanced air mobility | ~$25M | ~40x+ | ~20x | No |
| Intelligent Systems (INS) | Defence electronics, small-cap | ~$50M | ~2.0x | ~1.8x | Marginal |
| **Ondas Holdings (ONDS)** | **==Drone ISR (Ondas Networks deconsolidated Jan 2026)==** | **~~$35–50M~~ ==$50.7M FY2025 / $50.1M Q1 2026==** | **~~2.0–3.5x~~ ==~0x (cash > market cap)==** | **~~1.5–2.5x~~ ==~0x on $390M FY2026 target==** | **No** |

*Multiples estimated from public filings and consensus data as of May 2026. ~~ONDS figures based on range estimates described above.~~ ==ONDS TTM revenue reflects disclosed FY2025 and Q1 2026 results; forward target is management's May 14, 2026 guidance of at least $390 million against a $457 million pro forma backlog including Mistral and World View.== Joby included as a speculative-stage reference point only.*

The table illustrated ~~both the discount at which Ondas traded relative to pure-play defence drone peers and the risk premium still embedded in the forward multiple given execution uncertainty~~ ==how thoroughly the January 2026 cash raise had displaced operating-business valuation: at the May 2026 share-price band, the disclosed cash and short-term investments fully covered or exceeded the equity market capitalisation, leaving the operating EV/Sales multiple effectively at zero against both trailing and forward revenue==. AVAV's premium reflected a decade of DoD contract delivery; Ondas was still demonstrating that discipline. The Joby comparison was instructive in the other direction: pure-option speculative platforms could command enormous forward multiples, but Ondas' market appeared unwilling to price in that optionality ~~without near-term revenue evidence~~ ==even after management committed to a $390 million FY2026 target, treating the cash hoard rather than the operating outlook as the anchor==.

## What the Price Implies: A Reverse-DCF Frame

Approached from first principles rather than comparables, the question became: what revenue and margin trajectory did the market's current enterprise value imply? ~~At approximately $100 million EV—the midpoint of the estimated range—and applying a 10% long-run free-cash-flow margin assumption (conservative relative to AeroVironment's realised margins, but reasonable for a hardware-software defence platform at maturity), the terminal free cash flow required to justify today's price at a 10x FCF multiple was approximately $10 million annually. On a $35–50 million revenue base, reaching $10 million in free cash flow required roughly 20–25% net margins—achievable, but only after the current operating cost structure was restructured as revenue scaled. At a more optimistic 15% FCF margin, the breakeven revenue figure fell to approximately $65–70 million. The implication was pointed: the stock was pricing in limited multiple expansion and a relatively near-term path to cash-flow profitability, with almost no credit for the option value embedded in large-scale Western allied drone procurement contracts or a meaningful acceleration of the Ondas Networks rail deployment phase.~~ ==With operating enterprise value effectively at or below zero across the May 2026 share-price band—the disclosed $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments matching or exceeding the implied market capitalisation on 495,762,650 shares—the conventional reverse-DCF arithmetic inverted. The market was not pricing in a specific revenue or margin trajectory at all; it was pricing the balance-sheet cash as the dominant value and assigning the operating business close to zero. Even a 10% long-run free-cash-flow margin on the FY2025 base of $50.7 million implied roughly $5 million of terminal FCF, which would itself justify a small positive EV at a 10x multiple. Applying the same logic to the $390 million FY2026 target produced terminal FCF of roughly $39 million and a defensible operating EV of several hundred million dollars—virtually none of which the market was crediting. The implication had shifted from "limited room for multiple expansion" to "the market is heavily discounting management's target and assigning the option value of large-scale Western allied procurement to roughly nothing."==

## Bull, Base, and Bear Valuation Scenarios

Three scenarios framed the range of outcomes as of the frozen snapshot:

| Scenario | Key Assumptions | FY2026E Revenue | EV/Sales Applied | Implied EV | Implied Share Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | Israeli MoD multi-year framework contract; US DHS/DoD drone ISR programme award; ==Mistral/World View integration ahead of plan; Ondas Networks investment marked up== | ~~$90–110M~~ ==$450M+ (exceeds management target)== | 4.0x (AVAV discount narrows) | ~~$380–440M~~ ==~$1.8B operating EV + $1.48B cash== | ~~$8–10~~ ==~$6.50–7.00== |
| **Base** | Defence revenue converts at current trajectory; ==FY2026 target of at least $390M is met as Mistral/World View deliver on April 2026 close==; no major new platform wins | ~~$55–70M~~ ==~$390M (meets target)== | 2.5x | ~~$140–175M~~ ==~$975M operating EV + $1.48B cash== | ~~$3.00–4.00~~ ==~$4.90–5.10== |
| **Bear** | Revenue growth decelerates; ==Mistral/World View integration slips, FY2026 lands closer to $250M==; Israeli MoD engagement pauses amid geopolitical constraints; ~~ATM dilution continues; additional equity raise at depressed prices~~ ==cash burn accelerates against the January 2026 raise== | ~~$30–40M~~ ==~$250–300M== | 1.5x | ~~$45–60M~~ ==~$400M operating EV + $1.48B cash== | ~~$1.00–1.25~~ ==~$3.75–4.00 (cash floor dominates)== |

*Implied share prices based on ~~estimated 45 million diluted shares outstanding; EV-to-equity bridge assumes approximately $25 million net cash~~ ==495,762,650 shares outstanding as of May 13, 2026; EV-to-equity bridge applies the $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments disclosed in the Q1 2026 10-Q==. All figures approximate.*

The bull case required not merely revenue growth but a qualitative re-rating of the peer multiple: the market would need to award Ondas a discount to AVAV rather than the current premium discount. That demanded visible, repeatable DoD or allied-government contract delivery—not just Israeli MoD engagement—and a credible path to the Ondas Networks rail revenue recognising on a recurring basis. ==Equally striking was the bear case: even on a materially worse revenue outcome, the disclosed cash position established a price floor close to the prevailing trading range, meaning the asymmetry from the May 23, 2026 starting point skewed upward relative to a conventional pre-profit growth stock.==

## The Gap Between Consensus and the Dossier's Read

The consensus view, to the extent a coherent consensus existed for a stock with limited institutional coverage, appeared to price in the base scenario with a modest probability weighting toward the bull. The dossier's own read diverged on one key dimension: the Airobotics-Israeli MoD integration was underappreciated as a platform—not merely a customer—for broader defence export relationships in the Gulf, Eastern Europe, and Indo-Pacific theatres. The Optimus System's proven urban ISR deployment record in a live-conflict environment created a reference-customer narrative that no Western drone OEM could replicate from a standing start. An operator that had flown missions in and around active Iron Dome perimeters carried a proof-of-hardening that procurement officers in Warsaw, Tokyo, and Canberra would value. That option was not in the multiple. Whether it ever would be depended entirely on whether Eric Brock's team could convert Israeli MoD credibility into signed Western allied government contracts ~~before the ATM facility exhausted investor patience~~ ==while the $1.48 billion cash position bought multi-year runway to execute on the Mistral and World View integration and the $390 million FY2026 target==—and whether the rail side, slower and more certain, would provide enough cash-flow stability ==through the deconsolidated Ondas Networks investment== to fund the wait.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through American Robotics, Airobotics, and the defense ISR inflection
chapters.body:
## A company built in layers

The revenue record at Ondas ~~Holdings~~ ==Inc.== tells a story that is not linear. Between 2021 and 2025, the company assembled itself through acquisition, absorbed two wars, nearly ran out of cash, and then — almost without warning — delivered one of the most dramatic acceleration curves in the small-cap defence technology universe. Understanding the quarterly cadence requires holding three separate businesses in mind simultaneously: Ondas Networks, the rail communications business that predated everything else; American Robotics, bolted on in August 2021 to provide the drone-in-a-box platform; and Airobotics, acquired in January 2023, which brought both an Emirati commercial footprint and, through a subsequent asset purchase, the Iron Drone Raider counter-UAS system that ultimately became the company's primary revenue engine.

The numbers, arrayed across periods, capture the volatility of that construction process.

| Period | Revenue | Key Driver |
|--------|---------|------------|
| FY 2021 | $2.9M | Pre-Airobotics; American Robotics acquired August 2021 |
| FY 2022 | $2.1M | −28% YoY; Networks BNSF/CSX qualification; Q4 $0.5M |
| Q1 2023 | $2.6M | Airobotics acquisition closes January 2023 |
| Q2 2023 | $5.5M | UAE Optimus fleet orders; Siemens volume purchase order |
| Q3 2023 | $2.7M | October 7 attack; IIA awards $540K Iron Drone grant |
| Q4 2023 | $5.0M | Full-year $15.7M (+638% YoY); Networks $6.7M, OAS $9.0M |
| Q1 2024 | $0.6M | Initial Iron Drone PO from major Israeli defence company |
| Q2 2024 | ~$1.0M | Iron Drone orders from global defence and military customers begin |
| Q3 2024 | $1.5M | $14.4M bookings (Iron Drone $9M + Optimus $5.4M) |
| Q4 2024 | $4.1M | Full-year $7.2M (−54% YoY); OAS $5.3M, Networks $1.9M |
| Q3 2025 | $10.1M | Iron Drone in active military operations |
| Q4 2025 | $30.1M | Full-year $50.7M (+605% YoY); OAS $49.7M |

Sources: [FY2022](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/117/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2022) · [FY2023](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/155/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023) · [FY2024](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/199/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024) · [FY2025](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/296/ondas-inc-reports-record-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025)

## The construction years: 2022–2023

Full-year 2022 revenue of $2.1M — a decline from the $2.9M posted in 2021 — obscured meaningful commercial progress at Ondas Networks, where BNSF and CSX completed qualification testing of the FullMAX 900 MHz radio platform and Siemens placed its first volume purchase order. The headline number was shaped instead by the absence of meaningful drone revenue and by a $19.4M goodwill impairment charge that pushed the net loss to $73.2M for the year. The company ended 2022 with $29.8M in cash, supported by a $30M convertible note offering completed in October, giving it the runway to execute the acquisitions already in motion. [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/117/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2022)

At the early 2023 earnings call, three executives spoke in turn about what the coming year would deliver.

> "Ondas entered 2023 with momentum across all business segments. Our high-value, proprietary technology platforms have now transitioned to commercial adoption." — Eric Brock, Chairman & CEO, Q4 2022 earnings

> "Ondas Networks enters 2023 with growing momentum with commercial adoption of our FullMAX technology in the greenfield 900 MHz network." — Stewart Kantor, President, Ondas Networks

> "We have hit the ground running after closing the Airobotics acquisition in January and establishing the Ondas Autonomous Systems global business unit." — Meir Kliner, incoming OAS President

The optimism was not unreasonable in isolation. The Airobotics acquisition brought an operating Optimus drone platform with established commercial deployments in the United Arab Emirates, a government relationship in Israel, and an engineering team that would prove essential when Iron Drone Ltd.'s assets were folded in during March 2023. The Association of American Railroads' endorsement of IEEE 802.16t as the standard for 900 MHz rail networks, announced the same month, provided the external validation that Ondas Networks had been seeking for years. Q2 2023 revenue of $5.5M — the strongest quarter to that point — reflected UAE fleet orders and a Siemens volume purchase order for Indian Railways on-locomotive radios. Management guided publicly to full-year 2023 revenues of $26M to $30M. [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/155/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023)

The guidance did not survive contact with geopolitics. On 7 October 2023, Hamas launched its assault on southern Israel. Airobotics and Iron Drone engineering teams were headquartered in the country. Q3 2023 revenue came in at $2.7M. When Brock addressed investors that quarter, he led not with financial metrics but with an acknowledgment of the human situation.

> "I want to firstly highlight the remarkable courage displayed by our team in Israel in the midst of a challenging conflict." — Eric Brock, Q3 2023 earnings [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/142/ondas-holdings-reports-third-quarter-2023-financial-results)

> "Despite these challenges, we are more focused than ever on developing and delivering mission-critical solutions."

The full-year 2023 result of $15.7M — a 638% increase over 2022, driven by Ondas Autonomous Systems' $9.0M contribution and Networks' $6.7M — was simultaneously a landmark and a significant miss against guidance. Yet the Israel Innovation Authority had awarded a $540K grant for Iron Drone Raider development during Q3, signalling state-level confidence in the platform even as the conflict disrupted commercial timelines and the company burned cash to $15.0M at year-end from $29.8M twelve months earlier.

## The 2024 valley and the defence pivot

The first three quarters of 2024 recorded some of the lowest quarterly revenues in the company's post-acquisition history. Q1 came in at $0.6M — a figure that reflected the lag between Iron Drone's accelerated development cycle and its conversion into recognised revenue. Cash fell to $2.87M by the end of Q3 2024, a level that would normally prompt acute investor concern, and the company executed a series of equity and debt raises totalling $10.5M across those two quarters to maintain solvency. Full-year capital raised across 2024 reached $50.2M, comprising $38.4M in convertible and other debt, $7.4M in equity, and $4.4M from Ondas Networks preferred stock sales — a dilution cadence that had become the oxygen supply of the enterprise. [Source](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001646188/000121390025022968/ea0232702-10k_ondashold.htm)

The operational picture was diverging sharply from the reported revenue line. Iron Drone Raider had received an initial purchase order from a major Israeli defence company in Q1. Orders from a global defence firm and a major military customer followed in Q2. Then, in Q3 2024, management disclosed $14.4M in bookings — $9M in three separate Iron Drone orders placed between July and September, and $5.4M in Optimus orders for base and border security applications, all under programmes of record.

> "OAS secured multiple orders totaling $14.4 million for our Iron Drone Raider and Optimus System… The Iron Drone Raider system as a leading candidate to own the category for 'hard kill.'" — Eric Brock, Q3 2024 earnings [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/178/ondas-holdings-reports-third-quarter-2024-financial-results)

> "OAS had a pivotal quarter as evidenced with bookings of over $14 million… Iron Drone Raider system is emerging as a best-in-class counter drone solution." — Meir Kliner, OAS President, Q3 2024 earnings

Full-year 2024 revenue of $7.2M — a 54% decline from 2023 — represented the trough of the bookings-revenue divergence. Brock's year-end communication characterised 2025 as a pivot year in which OAS alone would contribute at least $20M against a company total of $25M.

> "2025 will be a record year with OAS expected to contribute at least $20 million in revenues of the expected Ondas Holdings revenue of $25 million." — Eric Brock, Q4 2024 earnings [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/199/ondas-holdings-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024)

> "2024 has been a transformative year for OAS, highlighted by record-breaking bookings." — Meir Kliner, Q4 2024 earnings

## The ISR inflection materialises: 2025

The guidance proved conservative by a factor of two. Q3 2025 revenue of $10.1M signalled that the backlog accumulated through the prior year was converting into deliveries, with Iron Drone Raider documented as operational in active military engagements. Q4 2025 delivered $30.1M — a single quarter larger than any full calendar year in the company's history. Full-year 2025 revenue reached $50.7M, a 605% year-on-year increase, with Ondas Autonomous Systems contributing $49.7M of that total. The balance-sheet transformation was equally striking: cash ended 2025 at $594.4M, reflecting $1.8B in gross equity raised since June 2025, with a further $960M in net proceeds from a January 2026 transaction completed after the frozen window. [Source](https://ir.ondas.com/press-releases/detail/296/ondas-inc-reports-record-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025)

> "2025 was a defining year for Ondas as we transitioned from a portfolio of advanced technologies into a scaled operating platform." — Eric Brock, FY2025 earnings

> "We exited the year with a significantly expanded backlog, reflecting accelerating global demand for our autonomous drone, counter-UAS and robotics solutions." — Oshri Lugassy, Co-CEO, Ondas Autonomous Systems

The backlog at year-end 2025 stood at $68.3M — before accounting for acquisitions of Sentrycs, Roboteam, Bird Aerospace, ~~and the announced Mistral transaction~~ ==Mistral, and World View==, all of which extended the addressable capability set across electronic warfare, ground robotics, cargo UAV, and sovereign manufacturing. Management ~~issued guidance of $375M or more for 2026~~ ==initially guided to FY2026 revenue of $375M or more and on May 14, 2026 raised the target to at least $390M==, a projection that, given the track record of the preceding three years, the market was obliged to evaluate with both the 2023 guidance miss and the 2025 guidance beat in hand simultaneously.

The quarterly cadence, taken whole, described not a clean growth curve but the uneven, often painful rhythm of a defence technology company finding its product-market fit in real time — and then, when conflict converged with capability, moving very fast indeed. Ondas Networks, meanwhile, ~~remained~~ ==was for years== the patient rail-infrastructure thread running beneath the drama: IEEE 802.16t progressing from AAR endorsement to multi-frequency adoption across 900 MHz, 450 MHz, and 160 MHz networks, with a first 160 MHz proof-of-concept installation completed in January 2026 and Amtrak deliveries tracking toward completion. The rail business never generated the revenue acceleration that early guidance implied, ~~but it outlasted every revision to the operating plan and retained its position as the segment most likely to compound steadily once Class I railroad procurement cycles finally aligned with Ondas's deployment calendar.~~ ==and a January 2026 capital restructuring deconsolidated Ondas Networks from the group altogether, with the Q1 2026 10-Q recording a gain on deconsolidation and derecognition of Networks assets and liabilities — so by the May 2026 snapshot, the rail thread sat outside the renamed Ondas Inc.'s consolidated results as a non-controlled affiliate rather than as a future compounding segment.==

chapters.title: Eric Brock, Reese Mozer, Israeli team, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## Eric A. Brock: Capital Allocator Turned Industrial-Technology Founder

Eric Allen Brock did not arrive at Ondas Holdings through a conventional operating-company path. Before assembling what became a dual-segment industrial technology platform, Brock spent roughly seventeen years as a professional investor, serving as a founding partner and portfolio manager at Clough Capital Partners, a Boston-based long-short equity and multi-asset investment firm he helped build from inception in 2000 through his departure in 2017. The practice of evaluating industrial cyclicals, critical-infrastructure capital spending, and emerging technology adoption from the buy side shaped the thesis he would later execute from the other side of the capital table.

His earlier career followed a more traditional formation: an accountancy training at Ernst & Young, followed by investment banking at Bear, Stearns & Co., before the transition to asset management. He holds an MBA from the University of Chicago and a BS from Boston College — credentials that, combined with the Clough tenure, positioned him more as a systematic capital allocator than as an operating executive. It was that background he brought to ~~the formation of Ondas Holdings in 2017 and the reverse-merger acquisition of Ondas Networks Inc. completed on~~ ==the reverse acquisition of Ondas Networks Inc. by Zev Ventures — the shell that changed its name to Ondas Holdings Inc. upon closing on== [September 28, 2018](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1646188/000121390026045735/ea0285575-02.htm).

From that date, Brock served as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the combined entity. His initial base salary under the employment agreement, signed the same day, was $200,000 per annum — modest for a public-company CEO and a figure that would remain largely static for years. During the COVID-19 disruptions of 2020, he accepted a 90% pay reduction from March through May, and a 35% reduction through mid-December, before salaries returned to prior levels. It was only in May 2025 that the compensation committee approved an increase to $400,000, effective 1 April 2025. The 2022 fiscal year proxy listed him owning approximately 1.89 million shares outright, giving him meaningful personal alignment with stockholders through a period of intense capital-markets activity.

Beyond the holding-company role, Brock accumulated subsidiary board and executive positions across every major acquisition: Chairman of Ondas Networks from September 2018; Chairman of American Robotics from August 2021; Chairman of Airobotics from January 2023; Co-Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Autonomous Systems from August 2024; and Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Capital from September 2025, the newly formed strategic investment and partnership unit. The accumulation reflected a deliberate, hands-on integration model rather than a decentralised holding-company architecture.

## Ondas Networks Segment: The Engineering Founders

The wireless segment arrived at Ondas Holdings as a going concern with its own technical roots. Menashe Shahar, who co-founded Ondas Networks, remained Chief Technology Officer through the period covered by the dossier, based at the company's Sunnyvale, California engineering offices. Shahar brought more than three decades of telecommunications system development experience to the FullMAX platform, including his work on broadband wireless deployments at WorldCom, Nortel, and ADC. He held multiple patents in data communications and had been an active participant in IEEE 802.16 standardisation activities — the technical lineage from which FullMAX was derived. His team at Sunnyvale concentrated through 2024 and 2025 on expanding the platform's applicability across the spectrum bands used by North American rail operators.

The commercial and operating leadership of the segment evolved. Stewart Kantor had served as President of Ondas Networks through the early years of the Ondas Holdings era, alongside Shahar on the technical side. By 2024, Markus Nottelmann had assumed the title of Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Networks, taking the segment's go-to-market leadership into the more intensive rail-deployment phase of the AAR 900 MHz private wireless initiative.

## American Robotics: Reese Mozer and the Founding Team's Short-Lived Corporate Tenure

American Robotics was co-founded in 2015 by Reese Mozer and Vijay Somandepalli, each bringing complementary credentialing to the venture. Mozer had spent four years, 2010 to 2014, at the Association for Unmanned Vehicle Systems International (AUVSI), researching commercial drone use cases, market gaps, and technology requirements at a time when the FAA regulatory framework for BVLOS automated operations was still nascent. A brief interlude at Palm Ventures, a private equity firm, supplemented his familiarity with growth-capital underwriting. By the time Ondas acquired American Robotics in August 2021, Mozer had also accumulated board-level positions at the Commercial Drone Alliance, the FAA Center of Excellence for UAS Research (ASSURE), and the Massachusetts Technology Leadership Council — a set of affiliations that underscored American Robotics' regulatory-vanguard positioning.

Somandepalli, the co-founder and CTO, held a PhD and master's degree in mechanical engineering from Stanford University and brought a decade-plus as a managing engineer at Exponent, the large scientific consulting firm, where he worked across oil and gas, solar, infrastructure, automotive, and aviation engagements. Inside Ondas he served as Vice President of Technical Strategy and as American Robotics' chief technology officer.
