Mozer's employment agreement with Ondas dated from the August 2021 acquisition. His formal integration into the corporate parent deepened in February 2023, when he was appointed President of Ondas Holdings — the number-two operational role — effective [February 14, 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1646188/000121390024028244/ea0202466-10k_ondashold.htm), just three weeks after the Airobotics close. The tenure proved brief: Mozer resigned on [June 8, 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1646188/000121390024028244/ea0202466-10k_ondashold.htm), forfeiting unvested option awards. His separation agreement waived the non-competition covenant to the extent it would have restricted him from entering the long-range cargo drones business — a carve-out that pointed toward his subsequent direction. Upon Mozer's departure, Brock absorbed the President title himself, holding Chairman, CEO, and President simultaneously from June 2023 onward.

## Israeli Integration: Meir Kliner and the Airobotics Founders

The January 2023 Airobotics acquisition brought an entirely distinct technical and cultural vector into the company. Meir Kliner, who had founded Airobotics and led development of the Optimus automated drone system since 2014, became President of what was then called Ondas Autonomous Systems, operating out of Petah Tikva in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area. Kliner's background spanned aerial-system design from recreational to military applications, and he had founded Light and Strong, a manufacturer of composite structures for drone airframes, prior to Airobotics — giving him deep supply-chain and materials expertise alongside his product-development credentials. The 2025 and 2026 10-K filings continued to identify him as President of OAS and as the head of the segment's research and development activities, supported by a development team that remained based primarily in Petah Tikva.

Oshri Lugassi joined Brock in a Co-Chief Executive Officer role at Ondas Autonomous Systems, an arrangement formalised by August 2024, bringing Israeli operational leadership to the joint-ventures and defence-customer engagement that had intensified after the October 2023 Gaza conflict.

The Israeli dimension of the executive roster introduced a directly observable geopolitical variable. Yishay Curelaru, who had been appointed Chief Financial Officer of Airobotics and of OAS in September 2023, was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces in October 2023 — weeks after the Hamas attack — temporarily stepping down from his CFO role before being re-appointed in January 2024 upon release from active duty. By 2025, Curelaru had been succeeded as CFO of OAS by Amit Bigler.

## The Corporate C-Suite: Laird and Huston

Neil Laird, 73, became the company's permanent Chief Financial Officer on [June 22, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1646188/000121390026045735/ea0285575-02.htm), having served as interim CFO from June 2024. His career traced a multi-decade arc through listed-company finance: CFO of ADAC Laboratories, a nuclear medicine and PET systems provider; CFO of SumTotal Systems, an enterprise learning management platform; and CFO of Mobileum Inc., a telecoms roaming and analytics business, from 2011 to 2016. He held an MA from the University of Cambridge and qualification as a UK chartered accountant — a credentialing profile more consistent with institutional finance than with Silicon Valley's equity-heavy compensation culture.

Patrick Huston, 57, joined the executive team as General Counsel in October 2025 and was appointed Chief Operating Officer and Secretary in December 2025 — completing Ondas's pivot toward defence market credibility. Huston retired from the United States Army as a general officer in September 2021 after a 35-year career that included service as a Commanding General, qualifications as an Army Ranger and helicopter pilot, and five combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan. He had served as General Counsel of the 101st Airborne Division, of JSOC (the Joint Special Operations Command), and of US Central Command — a set of roles that gave him an unusually direct line to the government procurement relationships OAS was seeking to develop. He also held FAA commercial pilot ratings and served on OAS's advisory board before his appointment to the corporate C-suite.

## Board Composition and the 2026 Proxy Structure

By the time of the 2026 annual meeting proxy, the Ondas board had contracted to four members from its earlier six-person composition after Thomas V. Bushey and Richard H. Silverman departed at the end of their 2023 terms. Silverman's departure was consequential: as the former General Manager of Salt River Project — one of the largest public power utilities in the United States, serving roughly one million customers in the Phoenix area — and as a past chair of both the Electric Power Research Institute and the Large Public Power Council, he had provided the board's most direct line to the utility and critical-infrastructure sectors that Ondas Networks sought to penetrate. His transition to "of counsel" at Jennings, Strouss & Salmon energy law practice left that sectoral expertise without a direct board successor.

The three independent directors remaining on the 2026 proxy slate each brought technology-sector rather than domain-operator backgrounds.

| Director | Age (2026) | Independence | Principal Affiliation | Key Background |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Richard M. Cohen | 75 | Independent | Richard M Cohen Consultants | Wharton BS, Stanford MBA, CPA; audit committee chair; serial micro-cap independent director |
| Randall P. Seidl | 62 | Independent | Rainwater Technologies (RAIN, CEO) | EMC employee #33; SVP HP Americas; SVP Sun Microsystems NA; Boston College |
| Jaspreet Sood | 52 | Independent | Palo Alto Networks (PANW) | 25 years HP/HPE; SVP Sales US Enterprise and Healthcare; Pepperdine MBA |

Cohen, appointed in September 2018 concurrently with the reverse merger close and having served on the Ondas Networks subsidiary board since April 2016, was the board's institutional memory and its audit-committee anchor. Seidl, who joined in November 2020, was the board's clearest technology-revenue and go-to-market voice — his career arc from EMC's earliest days through Hewlett-Packard's enterprise group and Sun Microsystems' North America business gave him pattern recognition on how technology platforms reached large enterprise and government customers. Sood, appointed January 2021 and the board's only woman, brought cybersecurity and enterprise-software go-to-market expertise accumulated across a quarter-century at Hewlett-Packard and its successor entities before joining Palo Alto Networks. The board's collective composition as of 2026 skewed toward capital markets and enterprise technology commercialisation rather than toward rail operations, defence procurement, or Israeli defence-technology ecosystems — a gap that, given the trajectory of OAS's customer base, represented a reasonable question for any prospective investor conducting governance analysis.

chapters.title: Class I freight railroads, Israeli MoD, Dubai/UAE, US public safety, commercial inspection
chapters.body:
## The Rail Corridor

Ondas Networks' commercial existence was, from its earliest deployable form, inseparable from the North American freight railroad. The company's FullMAX platform — a proprietary software-defined radio system derived from the IEEE 802.16 standard and purpose-engineered for the 900 MHz licensed spectrum band — found its natural first constituency in the seven Class I freight railroads that collectively operate the backbone of American surface freight. By the time Ondas Holdings completed its reverse-merger formation in ~~2017~~ ==2018, when Zev Ventures completed its reverse acquisition of Ondas Networks on September 28, 2018 and changed its name to Ondas Holdings Inc.==, the Association of American Railroads had already framed the commercial opportunity: a coordinated industry initiative to replace legacy narrowband wayside data systems with a higher-performance mission-critical private wireless network, the AAR Next Generation Higher-Performance Mission-Critical Data Communications System.

The six principal Class I engagement targets — Union Pacific, BNSF Railway, Norfolk Southern, CSX Transportation, Canadian National, and Canadian Pacific (post-merger with Kansas City Southern) — collectively operate tens of thousands of route-miles across the continental United States and Canada, each carrying positive train control obligations and an expanding appetite for automated wayside sensing, remote asset monitoring, and real-time operations data. The 900 MHz licensed band, allocated specifically for railroad use, gave Ondas Networks a regulatory moat that no unlicensed spectrum competitor could replicate. FullMAX's architecture — software-defined at the base station and endpoint, upgradeable over-the-air, and engineered to the AAR specification — positioned the company as the principal technology vendor available to fulfill the AAR's stated interoperability mandate.

The practical difficulty was timeline. AAR-coordinated industry initiatives operate on railroad timescales: procurement cycles measured in years, capital authorization processes layered through engineering, operations, and finance, and deployment sequencing tied to track-access windows and capacity planning. Through 2023 and into 2024, Ondas Networks continued advancing customer engagement with Class I railroad counterparties, but the revenue recognition cadence remained far slower than the commercial pipeline implied. Filings through this period consistently referenced the AAR initiative and ongoing customer trials without booking the large-scale deployment revenue that the addressable market arithmetic suggested. Rail remained ~~the company's~~ ==Ondas Networks'== longest-duration conviction story — substantial when it converts, uncertain on the quarter. ==In a January 2026 capital restructuring Ondas Holdings deconsolidated Ondas Networks, with the Q1 2026 10-Q recording a gain on deconsolidation and derecognition of Networks' assets and liabilities; the rail program continued inside the now-separately-capitalized Networks entity rather than as a consolidated Ondas Holdings segment.==

## The Israeli Ministry of Defense and Iron Dome Integration

The January 2023 acquisition of Airobotics introduced a customer base with an entirely different tempo. Airobotics' Optimus System — an automated drone-in-a-box platform operating without a human pilot at the point of flight — had been deployed by Israeli government security agencies before the acquisition, and the Israeli Ministry of Defense relationship sat at the center of the strategic rationale Ondas articulated when structuring the deal.

The Iron Dome air-defense network, Israel's layered missile-interception system, created demand for persistent low-altitude surveillance and threat-cueing assets that a ground-based radar-only architecture could not fully satisfy. Airobotics' automated drone platforms, capable of sustained perimeter and border surveillance without manual launch-and-recovery operations, aligned with the specific gap the Israeli security establishment sought to close: persistent aerial presence at the tactical edge, operated with minimal human overhead, and networked into a broader command-and-control layer. By the time the Ondas acquisition closed, Airobotics had already accumulated operational deployments with Israeli homeland security agencies and had positioned itself within the Israeli MoD's drone procurement framework.

Through 2023 and 2024, as the Gaza conflict sharply accelerated Israeli defense procurement and drew global attention to the operational utility of small autonomous drone systems, Ondas management highlighted the Airobotics Israeli MoD customer relationship as a central value-creation lever. The defense ISR demand inflection — driven simultaneously by the Ukraine war's demonstration of drone-centric warfare, the Israeli domestic demand surge, and the broader Indo-Pacific and Western allied procurement scaling — gave the Israeli MoD engagement a significance that transcended its direct revenue contribution. It served as proof-of-concept: a live, active sovereign customer operating Airobotics platforms in contested-environment adjacency, providing a reference that no amount of domestic US trials and pilot programs could substitute for.

## Dubai and the Gulf: Urban Drone Deployment

Parallel to its Israeli defense work, Airobotics had built a distinct and operationally distinct customer footprint in the Gulf: Dubai municipality and broader UAE government deployments of the Optimus System in urban surveillance and public safety roles. Dubai's aggressive posture toward drone technology adoption — anchored in the emirate's World Government Summit commitments and its long-standing ambition to operate autonomous aerial systems across the urban core — gave Airobotics an international flagship reference that differed materially from the Israeli defense use case.

The Dubai deployments were oriented toward traffic monitoring, public event security, and urban infrastructure inspection, with the Optimus System's automated dispatch and recovery capability enabling around-the-clock drone presence without the operational staffing burden that manual-pilot drone programs require. For Ondas, the Gulf footprint served a dual narrative function: it demonstrated that Airobotics' platform had cleared non-US regulatory and operational certification processes, and it opened a regional government customer segment that the company's American Robotics subsidiary had not penetrated. Gulf state sovereign wealth and municipal technology budgets represented a durable procurement channel independent of any single geopolitical event cycle.

## US Public Safety and Western Allied ISR: The Emerging Customer Base

Through 2024 and into 2025, Ondas Autonomous Systems worked to convert the defense ISR demand narrative into a US and Western allied customer base that could complement the Israeli and Gulf sovereign footprints. US public safety — municipal police departments, border patrol, emergency response agencies — represented the near-term domestic addressable market for the Optimus System's urban deployment capabilities, while Western allied defense ISR demand (NATO member procurement, Indo-Pacific US partner nations, US Department of Defense program engagement) represented the longer-arc strategic opportunity.

The FAA's evolving BVLOS regulatory framework was central to this effort. American Robotics had obtained the first FAA Part 107 waiver authorizing ~~fully automated~~ ==automated== BVLOS drone operations in 2021, ==with a subsequent January 2025 waiver permitting flights over people and moving vehicles from a centralized remote operations center, subject to waiver terms,== a regulatory milestone that neither Airobotics' Israeli certifications nor its Dubai approvals could substitute for in the US market. That waiver gave the combined Ondas Autonomous Systems entity a domestic operational authorization that most US drone-platform competitors had not yet cleared, and management consistently cited it as a differentiator in discussions with US defense and public safety procurement contacts.

The revenue conversion from this emerging customer base remained limited through the frozen-window date of May 2026, with the pipeline heavily weighted toward ongoing evaluation programs and limited initial deployment contracts rather than the large-scale procurement actions that AeroVironment (NASDAQ: AVAV) and other scaled defense drone primes had secured through established DoD program-of-record channels.

## Commercial Inspection: Scout System's Industrial Customer Base

American Robotics' Scout System addressed a fundamentally different customer segment: private-sector industrial operators requiring persistent automated inspection of distributed physical assets. Oil and gas pipeline operators, mining companies, rail Class II and Class III short-line operators, and utility infrastructure managers each faced variants of the same operational problem — remote or semi-remote assets requiring frequent visual and sensor inspection, manual inspection crews generating high cost and safety exposure, and regulatory compliance obligations demanding documentation cadences that legacy inspection methods could not economically sustain.

The Scout System's automated drone-in-a-box architecture — weatherproof ground station, automated launch and recovery, onboard AI-based defect detection, and cellular or satellite data backhaul — addressed this problem with minimal site staffing requirements. American Robotics had advanced commercial deployments with rail inspection customers, oil and gas operators, and mining sites through 2022 and 2023, with the BVLOS waiver enabling beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations that unlocked the full economic case for customers managing assets spread across miles of corridor or acreage.

| Customer Segment | Platform | Regulatory Anchor | Primary Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Class I freight railroads | FullMAX (Ondas Networks) | AAR 900 MHz licensed band | Mission-critical private wireless |
| Israeli MoD / homeland security | Optimus (Airobotics) | Israeli MoD approvals | Border surveillance, Iron Dome cueing |
| Dubai/UAE municipal | Optimus (Airobotics) | UAE civil aviation authority | Urban surveillance, public safety |
| US public safety / Western ISR | Optimus + Scout | FAA Part 107 BVLOS waiver | ISR, border, emergency response |
| Oil/gas, mining, rail Class II/III | Scout (American Robotics) | FAA Part 107 BVLOS waiver | Automated infrastructure inspection |
| Utility / energy private wireless | FullMAX (Ondas Networks) | Licensed spectrum (various) | Critical-infrastructure private wireless |

## Utility, Energy, and Broader Critical Infrastructure

Beyond rail, Ondas Networks' FullMAX platform carried an articulated value proposition for utility and energy private wireless applications: electric transmission and distribution operators, pipeline monitoring networks, and government critical-infrastructure operators all shared the Class I railroad's core requirement for licensed-spectrum, interference-resistant private wireless networks with deterministic latency and hardened security posture. The addressable market outside rail was substantially larger by route-mile than the railroad segment alone, though the AAR-coordinated industry initiative had provided a more concentrated procurement channel than the utility and energy sector's fragmented customer base offered.

Through the period ending May 2026, the utility and energy private wireless pipeline remained a stated commercial priority without having generated the concentrated customer relationships that the railroad engagement represented. The strategic logic was consistent: FullMAX's 802.16 architecture and licensed-band orientation gave Ondas Networks a technical profile that Nokia's and Ericsson's private wireless offerings — scaled for the enterprise and industrial Wi-Fi and CBRS market — had not prioritized. Whether that technical differentiation would translate into concentrated critical-infrastructure customer wins at the pace the addressable market implied remained the open variable in the Ondas Networks commercial thesis ==— a thesis that, following the January 2026 deconsolidation, ran through the standalone Networks entity rather than the Ondas Holdings consolidated group==.

chapters.title: Where ONDS sits against AVAV, Shield AI, Anduril, Skydio, and broader drone/private-wireless peers
chapters.body:
## A Company Without a Clean Peer

~~Ondas Holdings occupied~~ ==Ondas Inc. occupied== an unusual position in the technology investment universe: it was simultaneously too small to be a credible defense prime, too defense-adjacent to be dismissed as a pure commercial drone play, and too niche-focused to be evaluated against scaled private wireless infrastructure vendors. By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the company's dual-segment architecture — Ondas Networks' FullMAX rail private wireless platform and Ondas Autonomous Systems' Scout and Optimus drone-in-a-box fleets — put it in a competitive bracket of its own design, one where the moats were narrower but also harder to replicate than they appeared from the outside.

Understanding that position required mapping each segment against the relevant competitive set, acknowledging the scale gap honestly, and then identifying where the genuine barriers to entry actually resided.

---

## The Defense Drone Hierarchy

The most visible benchmarks for Ondas Autonomous Systems were the scaled US defense drone primes. AeroVironment (NASDAQ: AVAV), the Monrovia, California-based manufacturer of the Switchblade 300 and 600 loitering munitions alongside the Puma, Raven, and Wasp small tactical UAS platforms, reported revenue of approximately $717 million in its fiscal year ended April 2024, underwritten by a multi-year demand surge driven by Ukraine theater consumption and NATO allied force procurement. [AeroVironment FY2024 10-K, EDGAR] Kratos Defense & Security Solutions (NASDAQ: KTOS), developer of the XQ-58A Valkyrie high-performance unmanned combat air vehicle and a broader portfolio of aerial target drones, tracked approximately $1 billion in annual revenue by fiscal 2024. [Kratos FY2024 10-K, EDGAR]

Against those baselines, Ondas was not competing. Ondas Autonomous Systems was not pursuing US Air Force loyal-wingman contracts or selling Switchblade equivalents through the Foreign Military Sales pipeline. The comparison was a category error: AVAV and Kratos operated in the weapons system acquisition tier of the defense procurement hierarchy, while Ondas Autonomous Systems was positioning in the automated ISR and intelligence-gathering layer — persistently present, operationally autonomous, but fundamentally an information-collection platform rather than a kinetic-effects system.

| Company | Segment | FY2024 Revenue (approx.) | Primary platform |
|---|---|---|---|
| AeroVironment (AVAV) | Defense drone prime | ~$717M | Switchblade, Puma, Raven |
| Kratos (KTOS) | Defense drone prime | ~$1B | XQ-58A Valkyrie |
| ~~Ondas Holdings (ONDS)~~ ==Ondas Inc. (ONDS)== | Small-cap dual-segment | ~~Sub-$50M~~ ==~$7M== | Scout, Optimus, FullMAX |

The revenue gap was not a transitional deficiency to be closed by the next product cycle; it reflected a structural difference in what the companies were selling and to whom.

---

## Private Unicorns and the VC Arms Race

The more revealing competitive lens was the cohort of private defense-technology scale-ups that had received venture and growth-equity capital at multibillion-dollar valuations in the years following the 2022 Ukraine invasion.

Anduril Industries — founded in 2017 by Oculus co-founder Palmer Luckey and staffed heavily from Silicon Valley and defense program offices — raised capital in 2024 at a reported valuation approaching $14 billion, with a platform spanning the Altius-600 loitering munition, the Bolt autonomous air vehicle, and the Lattice operating system that served as an AI-fusion backbone across sensor networks. Shield AI, developer of the V-BAT vertical-takeoff-and-landing autonomous drone and the Hivemind machine-intelligence stack, closed a Series F in 2023 reportedly valuing the company at approximately $2.7 billion. Both Anduril and Shield AI were building toward a vision of fully autonomous multi-domain warfare software — not the inspection-and-surveillance drone-in-a-box category where Ondas Autonomous Systems competed.

Skydio, once the leading commercially-focused US autonomous drone manufacturer with the X2 and X10 platforms, provided a cautionary parallel. The San Mateo company had raised at a valuation of approximately $2.2 billion before executing a significant workforce reduction in late 2023 and pivoting heavily toward defense and law enforcement procurement channels. The difficulty Skydio encountered in scaling commercial enterprise inspection revenue before that pivot illustrated exactly the commercial-to-defense transition challenge that Ondas Autonomous Systems also faced — though Ondas entered the defense demand cycle with the Airobotics Israeli MoD relationship already in hand rather than building one from scratch.

---

## Commercial Inspection Peers

In the commercial automated inspection tier — oil-and-gas facilities, transmission-line corridors, mining sites, rail right-of-way — American Robotics' Scout System faced competition principally from Percepto, the Israeli-founded autonomous inspection platform whose "Sparrow" drone-in-a-box and Arc industrial software competed directly against Scout in upstream energy and critical-infrastructure applications. Easy Aerial, Flytrex, and Brinc addressed adjacent verticals (tethered surveillance, delivery logistics, and public-safety response respectively) without overlapping directly with Scout's primary commercial use case.

The decisive differentiator for American Robotics was regulatory: the company held the first Federal Aviation Administration Part 107.31 approval for fully automated drone flights beyond visual line of sight without a human remote pilot physically present at the site — a waiver category the FAA had not extended to any competitor as of the frozen snapshot date. That authorization, obtained in August 2021 and cited consistently in Ondas filings as a structural moat, meant American Robotics could offer commercial operators ~~the only legally sanctioned fully-unattended autonomous inspection flight in US airspace~~ ==the only legally sanctioned fully-unattended autonomous inspection flight in US airspace, subject to the waiver's operational terms==. Percepto, despite comparable technology, had not secured equivalent BVLOS authorization at the same autonomy tier by the frozen window.

The regulatory moat was not infinite in duration — the FAA's broader rulemaking toward a scaled BVLOS framework would, if completed, reduce the waiver scarcity premium. But through 2024-2026, the pioneering status remained operative and continued to frame American Robotics' commercial positioning in procurement conversations.

---

## The Israeli Defense Nexus

The acquisition of Airobotics positioned Ondas within an Israeli defense-technology ecosystem whose principal incumbents — Elbit Systems (NASDAQ: ESLT), Israel Aerospace Industries (state-owned), and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems (state-owned) — operated at an entirely different scale and mission profile.

Elbit, with annual revenues exceeding $5 billion and a Hermes-series MALE UAS portfolio deployed across five continents, was an Israeli defense prime in the conventional sense. IAI's Heron and Heron TP provided strategic-level unmanned reconnaissance; its Harop loitering munition entered operational service years before the Altius family. Rafael was a weapons-system developer whose Iron Dome interceptor battery was the principal technology against which Airobotics' border-surveillance Optimus deployments were integrated — a cooperative relationship, not a competitive one.

Airobotics' role in the Israeli defense ecosystem was as an automated urban surveillance and perimeter-security platform, providing persistent aerial situational awareness at border sites and critical installations. That function was complementary to what IAI and Rafael built rather than competitive with it. The Ondas/Airobotics relationship to the Israeli MoD should have been read as sub-prime or specialist contractor, not as a rival to Elbit's scale: a supplier of automated ground-station-to-air capabilities that the larger primes did not offer in production form.

---

## Private Wireless: A Different Kind of Moat

Ondas Networks' FullMAX platform did not compete with Nokia (HEX: NOKIA) or Ericsson (STO: ERIC.B) for enterprise private 5G contracts at automobile plants or port terminals. Nokia's Digital Automation Cloud and Ericsson's Dedicated Networks product lines had each deployed hundreds of private wireless networks globally across manufacturing, logistics, and mining verticals by 2024. Cisco provided overlay networking and security infrastructure across many of the same deployments.

The FullMAX competitive perimeter was deliberately narrower. The platform targeted the 900 MHz licensed spectrum band allocated to the US rail industry under the Association of American Railroads' Next Generation Higher-Performance Mission-Critical Data Communications System initiative — a frequency-specific, use-case-specific, industry-coordinated procurement process for which the broader Nokia and Ericsson product portfolios were not architected. The AAR initiative functioned as a coordinated industry standard rather than an open competitive RFP, and Ondas Networks' positioning as the designated technology partner within that initiative represented a structural advantage that did not map cleanly onto conventional telecom-vendor competitive analysis.

---

## Synthesis: The Niche Stack Thesis

Taken together, ~~Ondas Holdings by May 2026~~ ==Ondas Inc. by May 2026== was best understood not as a company failing to scale to the size of its apparent competitors, but as one that had deliberately carved three narrow regulatory and relationship-based positions: the only holder of FAA full-BVLOS autonomous drone approval in US commercial airspace; the only US-listed small-cap with a production-deployed autonomous urban drone platform integrated into Israeli MoD and Iron Dome border-security infrastructure; and the designated technology partner for the AAR rail-industry coordinated private wireless initiative in the US 900 MHz band.

Each of those positions was genuinely defensible for a defined period. None of them was scalable to AVAV revenue levels on a three-year horizon. The strategic question for investors, therefore, was whether the three niches could be monetized at a pace that justified the capital consumption profile — a question about execution and timing, not about whether the competitive moats existed at all.

chapters.title: Timeline from 2017 formation through 2023-2025 defense ISR inflection
chapters.body:
## The Reverse Merger That Started Everything

Ondas Holdings did not begin life as a drone company. When Eric Brock engineered ~~the corporate parent's formation through a reverse merger in 2017~~ ==the corporate parent's formation through the reverse acquisition that closed September 28, 2018, when Zev Ventures changed its name to Ondas Holdings Inc.==, the vehicle he assembled was built around a single proprietary asset: the FullMAX software-defined radio platform, a derivative of the IEEE 802.16 wireless standard tuned for the 900 MHz licensed spectrum that the Association of American Railroads had designated for its Next Generation Higher-Performance Mission-Critical Data Communications System initiative.

The logic was straightforward and unsexy. Class I freight railroads — Union Pacific, BNSF, Norfolk Southern, CSX, Canadian National, Canadian Pacific — operated on aging digital radio networks that could not support the sensor density, remote-monitoring throughput, or safety-automation requirements that the industry's modernization agenda demanded. The AAR had coordinated a spectrum allocation specifically for that purpose. Ondas Networks, the principal operating subsidiary, held what Brock argued was the only purpose-built software-defined radio stack tuned for that band.

For the first several years of the company's public life, that thesis was the whole investment case. The stock was thinly traded, the revenue base was in the low single-digit millions, and the operating losses were large relative to any tangible commercial traction. Brock positioned Ondas as a picks-and-shovels play on a secular rail modernization cycle: not a systems integrator or a rolling-stock manufacturer, but the wireless infrastructure layer that every major freight railroad would eventually need. Whether that conversion from design-win pipeline to contracted deployment would arrive in 2021, 2022, or later was the central investor question the company spent years unable to resolve with precision.

## American Robotics and the Pivot to Autonomous Systems

The strategic narrative shifted materially in August 2021, when Ondas announced the acquisition of American Robotics, a Marlborough, Massachusetts-based startup that had built the Scout System — an automated drone-in-a-box platform designed for persistent, repeatable aerial inspection of linear infrastructure including oil and gas pipelines, rail corridors, and mining operations.

American Robotics was not simply another commercial drone startup. The company had secured what was at the time an industry-first: a Federal Aviation Administration exemption allowing fully automated, beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations under Part 107 without a human observer present at the launch site. That regulatory milestone, obtained in December 2020, gave American Robotics a moat that competitors with more capital but less FAA engagement had not replicated. Reese Mozer, the company's founder, had built the regulatory case alongside the hardware, and the combination positioned Scout as the closest thing the commercial drone market had to an FAA-blessed autonomous inspection product.

For Brock, the acquisition served two purposes simultaneously. It gave Ondas a second revenue segment with genuine commercial deployments — initial Scout customers included oil and gas operators and rail infrastructure owners — and it repositioned the parent company's narrative from a single-product private wireless play to a diversified autonomous-systems and critical-infrastructure technology platform. The stock market responded accordingly: Ondas' market capitalisation moved meaningfully higher through the second half of 2021 as the drone-sector enthusiasm that had lifted companies such as AeroVironment and a raft of SPAC-listed drone entrants provided a favorable backdrop.

## Airobotics and the Israeli MoD Franchise

If American Robotics was a commercial inspection story with regulatory upside, the Airobotics acquisition announced in January 2023 was something categorically different: it brought a live Israeli Ministry of Defense customer relationship, Iron Dome border-security integration disclosures, and a track record of municipal drone deployments across Dubai and the broader UAE into the Ondas portfolio.

Airobotics, founded and headquartered in Petah Tikva, Israel, had developed the Optimus System — an urban automated drone platform designed for perimeter security, situational awareness, and rapid response in high-density environments. The company's principal customers were not commercial inspection operators but sovereign governments: the Israeli MoD and its associated homeland security agencies, and the Dubai municipality, which had deployed Optimus across infrastructure monitoring and emergency response applications.

The acquisition closed as the broader defense and security environment was about to shift dramatically. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 had already demonstrated that small autonomous aerial systems could reshape ground warfare at a fraction of the cost of conventional weapons programmes. By late 2022 and into 2023, every Western defence ministry was accelerating procurement reviews for uncrewed aerial systems. Israel's own operational experience, both in border surveillance and in the evolving conflict environment that would intensify sharply after October 2023, created an accelerating demand signal for exactly the kind of urban-persistent-surveillance capability that Airobotics had spent years productising.

Meir Kliner and the Airobotics leadership team were integrated into what Ondas reorganised as its Ondas Autonomous Systems segment — combining American Robotics' US commercial franchise with Airobotics' Israeli and Gulf State government franchise under a unified segment structure. The operational headquarters remained bifurcated: Marlborough, Massachusetts for American Robotics and Petah Tikva for the Israeli operations.

## The ISR Demand Inflection, 2023–2025

The period from early 2023 through the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 constituted the most consequential demand inflection in Ondas Autonomous Systems' short history. Three independent drivers converged.

The first was the Israel-Gaza conflict, which began in October 2023 and drove an immediate acceleration in Israeli MoD procurement of autonomous aerial surveillance systems. Airobotics' existing relationship with Israeli defence and homeland security agencies positioned it as a qualified domestic supplier at a moment when procurement cycles compressed from years to months. Israeli MoD engagement disclosures through 2024 and into 2025 became the single most watched catalyst in Ondas' investment narrative.

The second was the broader Western allied drone procurement scaling driven by the Ukraine experience and Indo-Pacific threat reassessments. NATO member states, Gulf allies, and US public safety agencies were all evaluating drone-in-a-box platforms for persistent surveillance applications. Airobotics' existing Dubai municipal deployment record and American Robotics' FAA BVLOS waiver legacy gave Ondas a credible case for inclusion in procurement shortlists that purely notional or unfunded competitors could not match.

The third was the continued maturation of the Ondas Networks rail deployment pipeline. The AAR-coordinated 900 MHz initiative moved through vendor qualification and pilot deployment phases across the 2023–2025 period, with Class I railroad engagement providing the reference deployments that the FullMAX commercial case had long required.

| Milestone | Date | Segment |
|---|---|---|
| Corporate parent formation (reverse merger) | ~~2017~~ ==2018== | Corporate |
| American Robotics acquisition | August 2021 | Autonomous Systems |
| FAA Part 107 BVLOS waiver (American Robotics) | December 2020 | Autonomous Systems |
| Airobotics acquisition | January 2023 | Autonomous Systems |
| Israeli MoD engagement disclosures | 2023–2025 | Autonomous Systems |
| Rail private wireless pilot deployments (AAR initiative) | 2023–2025 | Ondas Networks |

Capital structure throughout this period was funded principally through at-the-market equity offerings and registered direct transactions. The ATM facility gave management flexibility to draw capital against market conditions but created a persistent dilution overhang that the investor base priced accordingly. ~~Cash runway cadence and the timing of defense contract award conversions — from disclosed engagement to booked revenue — remained the defining variables in the investment thesis through the frozen snapshot date.~~ ==That overhang was resolved in January 2026 with a financing that left Ondas reporting $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments at March 31, 2026, after which the defining variable in the investment thesis narrowed to the timing of defense contract award conversions from disclosed engagement to booked revenue.==

## Forward Catalysts

As of May 2026, the forward catalyst set for Ondas was concentrated in four areas. The most immediate was the conversion of Israeli MoD engagement into confirmed multi-year programme contracts, where disclosed relationships had not yet translated into the revenue run-rate that the demand environment logically implied. The second was US public safety drone deployment: American Robotics' BVLOS-waiver platform was positioned for police aviation, border patrol, and infrastructure monitoring contracts that the US government drone procurement build-out was beginning to fund in earnest. The third was the Ondas Networks rail deployment timeline — the AAR initiative had sufficient Class I railroad commitment to suggest the first full commercial network deployments were approaching, ~~and the revenue conversion from pilot to programme would represent the first material Ondas Networks contribution to consolidated results~~ ==though the January 2026 Ondas Networks capital restructuring deconsolidated the rail subsidiary from Ondas Inc.'s financial reporting, so any revenue conversion from pilot to programme would now sit outside the parent's consolidated results==. The fourth was broader Western allied procurement participation: UK, Australian, and other Five Eyes-adjacent defence procurement programmes were evaluating small-UAS persistent surveillance platforms against specifications that Airobotics' Optimus System was built to meet. ~~Whether Ondas' capital structure — and Brock's capacity to fund inventory build ahead of contract delivery — could absorb the working-capital demands of scaling all four simultaneously was the question that would define the 2026 chapter of the company's history.~~ ==With $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments on the Q1 2026 balance sheet, the question that would define the 2026 chapter of the company's history was no longer capital capacity but Brock's execution speed in converting the disclosed engagement pipeline into the booked revenue that the at least $390 million FY2026 target implied.==

chapters.title: FullMAX dot16, Scout System IP, Optimus System IP, drone autonomy
chapters.body:
## The Wireless Foundation: FullMAX and the 802.16 Lineage

Ondas Networks was built on a single technical proposition: that the IEEE 802.16 standard, best known as the backbone of WiMAX broadband deployments, could be re-engineered as a deterministic, low-latency private wireless protocol suited to the licensed 900 MHz spectrum the Association of American Railroads had reserved for next-generation mission-critical data communications. The result was FullMAX, a software-defined radio platform that Ondas developed and retained as wholly owned proprietary IP from the company's earliest operating years.

The 802.16 derivation was not incidental. Where commercial WiMAX prioritized throughput for internet broadband, Ondas's engineering team adapted the MAC and physical layers to emphasize the qualities rail operations required: deterministic message delivery, robust performance in electrically noisy right-of-way environments, and the ability to prioritize safety-of-life control messages over bulk telemetry. The software-defined architecture meant that firmware updates — rather than hardware replacement — could extend the platform's capabilities as the AAR's coordinated industry initiative evolved its technical specifications. That upgrade-in-field characteristic became a material competitive differentiator when Ondas pitched Class I freight railroads that had already committed to 900 MHz licensed spectrum infrastructure and needed to protect the capital deployed in base-station buildouts.

The patent and trade-secret framework around FullMAX encompassed the core waveform design, the proprietary scheduling algorithms that governed how the system managed contention among hundreds of simultaneous endpoints across a wayside network, and the software stack enabling interoperability with Class I railroad operational technology platforms. Because the AAR's initiative required multi-vendor interoperability testing, Ondas had to protect the differentiated layer of the stack — the performance and reliability envelope — rather than a closed end-to-end stack, a discipline that sharpened the boundaries of what the company actually owned versus what it implemented to a published standard.

## Scout System: The FAA Waiver as IP Complement

The August 2021 acquisition of American Robotics brought Ondas a second and structurally distinct body of intellectual property. The Scout System was an automated drone-in-a-box: a ground-based docking station housing a small fixed-wing-hybrid or multirotor drone that could autonomously launch, execute a pre-planned inspection flight, return, recharge, and await the next mission cycle — without a licensed pilot present on-site. The hardware and mechanical design of the dock, including its weatherproofing, drone capture mechanism, and battery management system, formed one layer of protectable IP.

The deeper asset, however, was regulatory rather than purely technical. American Robotics became the first company to receive an FAA Part 107 waiver ~~permitting fully autonomous beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone operations without a human visual observer, a landmark clearance the agency granted in 2021~~ ==permitting beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone operations without a human visual observer subject to specified waiver terms, a landmark clearance the agency granted in 2021== after an extended data-collection and safety-case review process. The operational data underlying that waiver — flight performance logs, failure-mode analysis, the software safety architecture demonstrating deterministic return-to-home behavior under communications loss or geofence violation — constituted a trade-secret corpus that would be expensive and time-consuming for a competitor to replicate from scratch. The waiver itself was non-transferable, but the institutional knowledge embedded in the application process, and the iterative software development history it reflected, sat squarely inside American Robotics' IP estate when Ondas acquired the company.

American Robotics had targeted commercial inspection verticals — oil and gas pipeline corridors, rail infrastructure, mining sites, utility rights-of-way — where repetitive, scheduled surveillance over large fixed footprints mapped precisely to the Scout System's autonomous-repeat-mission architecture. The mission-planning software, which generated optimized flight paths from GIS layers and customer asset maps, and the analytics pipeline that converted raw sensor imagery into structured inspection reports, were developed and owned by the company. Ondas's 10-K filings described these software capabilities as internally developed, with the underlying algorithms and training datasets treated as trade secrets rather than patented inventions.

## Optimus System: Urban Autonomy and the Airobotics Lineage

The January 2023 acquisition of Airobotics added a complementary but technically distinct IP tree. The Optimus System was designed for urban and peri-urban operating environments — municipal surveillance, port and border security, large venue monitoring — where the duty cycle demanded was higher than commercial inspection applications and the regulatory and political context required a platform hardened for sensitive-site proximity.

Airobotics' signature engineering achievement was its robotic payload and battery exchange mechanism: a dock-integrated robotic arm that could swap both the battery pack and the sensor payload between missions, enabling a single ground station to sustain near-continuous airborne presence through sequential sorties. The mechanical design of that exchange system, the software coordinating the arm's motion with the drone's docking approach sequence, and the sensor-agnostic payload interface that allowed the platform to carry EO/IR, multispectral, or LiDAR pods under the same software management layer were the core protectable innovations the Israeli engineering team had developed since Airobotics' founding.

The Optimus System's operational history in Israel — including deployments supporting Israeli Ministry of Defense surveillance requirements and integration into border-security infrastructure associated with Iron Dome perimeter coverage — generated a second trade-secret corpus: the mission-management software logic tuned for Israeli regulatory and operational requirements, the RF and electromagnetic compatibility characterizations from operations in dense urban environments, and the safety-case documentation that had satisfied Israeli civil aviation authority scrutiny for urban BVLOS. That body of documented operational experience, alongside the relationships with Israeli defense procurement offices, was what Ondas was acquiring in addition to hardware blueprints and software source code.

## Autonomy Layer: Sensor Fusion and AI Analytics

Sitting above both platform-specific IP estates was a shared autonomy software layer that Ondas was developing, by 2024, as a common capability across the Scout and Optimus platforms. The layer encompassed multi-sensor fusion — combining visual, thermal, and LiDAR inputs into a coherent situational picture — AI-driven anomaly detection trained on labeled inspection and surveillance datasets, and adaptive mission-replanning logic that could reroute an airborne drone in response to airspace conflicts or sensor-identified objects of interest.

The fusion architecture was particularly relevant to defense ISR positioning. Military end users required not raw imagery but derived intelligence products — structured detections, track histories, change maps — generated autonomously aboard or immediately post-mission. Ondas's ability to claim that the analytics layer was proprietary, built on internally owned training data from commercial deployments, distinguished its pitch from integrators reselling commodity hardware running open-source inference frameworks. The commercial deployment history — thousands of autonomous Scout System sorties over US industrial sites — provided a labeled dataset depth that a new entrant would need years to assemble independently, underpinning a network-effect advantage that reinforced the formal patent and trade-secret protections.

chapters.title: Pre-profit execution, dilution, defense program timing, Israel geopolitical, competitive, scale
chapters.body:
## The Gap Between Narrative and Revenue

The most persistent structural risk confronting Ondas Holdings entering the back half of the 2020s was not technological — the Scout System's FAA BVLOS waivers were real, the Optimus System's Israeli MoD deployments were documented, and the FullMAX radio platform had survived a decade of railroad skepticism to reach commercial deployment. The risk was temporal: the distance between a compelling strategic narrative and recurring, contract-backed revenue, measured in quarters and dilutive share counts.

Eric Brock assembled a two-segment platform — Ondas Networks servicing the 900 MHz rail private wireless initiative and Ondas Autonomous Systems deploying automated drone platforms through American Robotics and Airobotics — at precisely the moment when Western defense procurement was accelerating fastest. The problem was that "precisely the moment" in defense procurement means something different than it does in commercial software. Program cycles measured in years, approval chains layered through multiple sovereign governments, and inventory build requirements that consume cash well ahead of delivery receipts all compressed the gap between strategic opportunity and financial execution risk into something acute for a company funded primarily by equity issuance.

## Pre-Profit Execution and the Defense Revenue Conversion Lag

Ondas Holdings entered the ~~2023–2026 period as a pre-profit platform generating revenue in the low double-digit USD millions range annually~~ ==2023–2024 period as a pre-profit platform generating revenue in the low double-digit USD millions range annually, with FY2025 revenue then scaling to $50.7 million and Q1 2026 revenue alone reaching $50.1 million== — a scale mismatch against the capital intensity of integrating two acquisition targets while simultaneously ramping commercial deployments across railroads, Israeli homeland security agencies, and Gulf state municipalities. Operating losses funded R&D, integration overhead, and the inventory required to fulfill emerging defense ISR contracts, and those losses were chronic rather than transitional.

The defense ISR demand inflection driven by Ukraine, the Gaza conflict, and Indo-Pacific tensions generated genuine pipeline — but pipeline in defense is not revenue. From initial program identification through proposal, evaluation, contracting, delivery, and final acceptance, a defense drone program routinely spans 18 to 36 months or longer. For a company operating on a quarterly cash-burn cadence and reliant on equity markets to fund operations, that conversion lag created a persistent mismatch. Each quarter in which pipeline did not convert to recognized revenue was a quarter in which dilution machinery ran while the revenue narrative deferred.

The Airobotics integration compounded this. The January 2023 acquisition imported an Israeli operational infrastructure — Petah Tikva development team, Israeli MoD relationships, UAE municipal deployments — onto a US-listed small-cap balance sheet that bore acquisition-related goodwill and intangible assets requiring ongoing impairment assessment. Should defense program timelines slip or Israeli government procurement priorities shift, the carrying values assembled through acquisition accounting would face pressure at precisely the moment when investor patience was already strained.

## Dilution Risk and the ATM Mechanism

Ondas' capital structure through 2024–2025 rested on a foundation of at-the-market equity offerings and registered direct placements. The ATM facility provided flexibility — capital could be raised incrementally against the prevailing share price without the discount mechanics of a traditional block offering — but it also meant that every quarter of operating losses translated directly into share count expansion and per-share dilution for existing holders.

The mechanism is structurally corrosive at small-cap scale. When the share price reflects a defense-program narrative ahead of actual contract flow, ATM issuance raises capital at valuations that compress the moment sentiment shifts. When contract announcements arrive and the stock re-rates upward, dilution has already occurred at lower prices. The round-trip — burn cash at sub-contract valuations, issue equity, announce program, watch stock recover, repeat — erodes the compounding benefit of each strategic milestone for long-duration holders.

Ondas' investor base by the mid-2020s was consequently exposed to a dual risk: execution against program milestones on one axis, and the cadence and pricing of equity issuance on the other. Neither variable was entirely within management's control. ==The January 2026 financing materially altered the near-term cadence of this dynamic: Q1 2026 disclosed approximately $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash, and short-term investments, removing immediate reliance on incremental equity issuance even as cumulative share count had moved from roughly 93 million at December 31, 2024 to approximately 495.8 million outstanding by May 13, 2026.==

## Defense Program Timing Volatility

No sector rewards optimism about program timing more persistently — or punishes it more harshly — than defense procurement. The demand signals driving Ondas Autonomous Systems' ISR positioning were real: Western allied governments accelerating drone procurement, the Israeli government operating in a sustained multi-front security posture, and the UAE municipal drone infrastructure build continuing through Gulf state modernization programs. But demand signals are not contracts, contracts are not deliveries, and deliveries are not revenue.

Defense program timing risk at Ondas manifested across several dimensions simultaneously. On the Israeli MoD side, procurement decisions embedded within Iron Dome and broader border-security programs moved through approval processes that reflected domestic political dynamics, parliamentary budget cycles, and coalition-government stability — none of which Ondas could influence. On the US allied side, the emerging public-safety and defense ISR customer base that Airobotics and American Robotics were collectively cultivating through 2024–2026 was subject to federal appropriations timing, regulatory body adjudication of BVLOS operational frameworks, and interagency coordination requirements that extended program timelines beyond commercial expectations.

The result was a revenue profile with meaningful lumpiness risk — individual large contracts could materially move quarterly figures in both directions, and the absence of a diversified, recurring-revenue base meant that a single program delay could reset the trajectory investors had been pricing.

## Israel Geopolitical Risk

The January 2023 acquisition of Airobotics imported a structural geopolitical variable into the Ondas balance sheet that had no counterpart in the American Robotics or Ondas Networks operations. Airobotics' principal development and operational infrastructure sat in Petah Tikva, Israel. Its core customer relationships ran through the Israeli Ministry of Defense and Israeli homeland security agencies. The October 7, 2023, Hamas attack and the subsequent Gaza conflict — ongoing through the frozen snapshot date — placed those operations in a sustained elevated-risk environment.

The operational continuity of the Petah Tikva team through the conflict was a genuine achievement, and the Israeli security posture arguably accelerated certain procurement timelines for border-surveillance drone systems. But the geopolitical risk cut in multiple directions. Israeli defense budgets under sustained wartime mobilization faced competing claims from kinetic weapons systems, manpower, and logistics that could redirect procurement away from autonomous drone platforms. Israeli export-control frameworks governing drone technology tightened materially through 2024–2025 as the government managed dual-use technology flows, potentially constraining Airobotics' ability to expand into third-country markets. And any escalation into a regional conflict involving Iran or Lebanese Hezbollah introduced potential physical infrastructure risk to Ondas' Israeli operations that no insurance framework could fully price.

## Competitive Intensity: Scaled Primes and Well-Funded Challengers

The competitive environment Ondas entered as a defense-drone aspirant was populated by adversaries operating at fundamentally different resource scales.

| Competitor | Status | Key advantage |
|---|---|---|
| AeroVironment (AVAV) | Public (NASDAQ) | Decade of DoD contract flow, Switchblade program, established procurement relationships |
| Anduril | Private, $14B+ valuation | Software-defined defense platform, Lattice OS, scaled government relations |
| Shield AI | Private, $2.7B+ valuation | F-16 AI pilot, autonomous air-to-air capability, USAF embedded relationships |
| Skydio | Private | Domestic manufacture, Blue UAS framework, US DOD supply-chain preference |

Against this competitive set, Ondas' differentiators — the Optimus System's urban autonomous infrastructure, the Scout System's FAA BVLOS waiver stack, and the Israeli MoD's operational validation of Airobotics in live border-security deployments — were genuine but narrow. AeroVironment entered the mid-2020s with a revenue base an order of magnitude larger than Ondas, a Switchblade loitering munitions program that had received sustained Congressional support, and procurement relationships built over more than a decade of DoD engagement. Anduril and Shield AI, though private, had raised capital at valuations that enabled talent acquisition, hardware iteration cycles, and government-relations infrastructure unavailable to a NASDAQ small-cap running on ATM-funded quarters.

The Blue UAS framework — the US Department of Defense's preferred domestic supply-chain certification pathway — represented a particular structural challenge. Ondas' Airobotics operations were headquartered in Israel, meaning the supply-chain provenance requirements for sensitive DoD programs would require either a domestic manufacturing transition or a partnership structure that could dilute program economics.

## Small-Cap Scale Constraints

Ondas Holdings entered the critical 2024–2026 window as a NASDAQ small-cap with the organizational surface area of a mid-size technology business — two operating segments, three geographic footprints, a dual-track commercial and defense customer engagement strategy, and an engineering team split across Massachusetts and Petah Tikva. The management bandwidth required to simultaneously advance the FullMAX rail deployment, scale American Robotics' commercial inspection business, integrate and grow the Airobotics Israeli and UAE operations, and cultivate a nascent US defense ISR pipeline exceeded what the resource base could absorb without execution risk.

Small-cap scale also constrained investor optics. Extreme share-price volatility — driven by contract announcements, Israeli MoD engagement disclosures, and drone-sector sentiment — made Ondas an unsuitable holding for institutional capital with volatility mandates, narrowing the potential shareholder base and making the stock susceptible to retail momentum swings that bore little relationship to underlying program execution. Each capital raise into a down-trending share price tightened that constraint further, eroding the equity currency available to fund the next phase of the very strategy that justified the premium valuation.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## A thin bench, a loaded calendar

Ondas Holdings enters its next twelve-month stretch with a characteristic combination of micro-cap illiquidity and macro-level tailwinds. Formal sell-side coverage remains sparse — fewer than four active analysts issue price targets on the stock at the frozen snapshot — which means any single contract announcement or guidance revision can produce outsized price dislocations in both directions. The practical implication for an investor holding through this window is that price discovery will be driven more by episodic disclosure events than by any smoothly updating consensus model.

The catalyst calendar from Q2 2026 through Q1 2027 is unusually dense for a company of this market capitalization, spanning defense contract renewals, a nascent rail wireless deployment ramp, autonomous drone commercial scaling, and a capital structure that demands periodic attention to dilution pace.

## Quarter-by-quarter catalyst timeline

**Q2 2026 results (anticipated August 2026).** The Q2 print will be the first full quarter following the recently completed Q1 2026 report. The primary variable is Ondas Autonomous Systems' revenue recognition from Israeli Ministry of Defense–related engagements. Airobotics' Optimus System deployments in Israeli border-security and urban-surveillance contexts have been the headline revenue driver since the January 2023 acquisition. By Q2 2026, investors will be watching whether Israeli MoD procurement — which accelerated sharply through 2024–2025 on the back of the Gaza conflict and broader homeland-security demand — has translated into a durable booking cadence ~~or whether Q4 2025 represented a one-time recognition event~~ ==or whether the Q1 2026 step-up to $50.1 million in quarterly revenue sustains into Q2==. A secondary watch item is the Ondas Networks rail wireless deployment schedule: any update from Class I railroad partners on field-trial progression within the AAR 900 MHz coordinated industry initiative will be closely parsed.

**Q3 2026 results (anticipated November 2026).** The third quarter is the critical hinge point for full-year 2026 guidance credibility. ~~Management has historically provided qualitative directional guidance rather than hard numeric ranges; if Q3 revenue does not track toward a cadence consistent with the year's implied growth rate, sell-side models will be marked down materially ahead of the December year-end.~~ ==Management's May 14, 2026 raise of the FY2026 revenue target to at least $390 million makes Q3 the quarter where revenue cadence must visibly track toward that bar; any meaningful shortfall will force sell-side models down materially ahead of the December year-end.== The specific milestone to watch in this window is any Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) or US Army program-of-record announcement that names an Ondas or American Robotics platform — such disclosures have been cited as a potential catalyst in company presentations and would represent a structural step-change from the current Israeli-centric revenue base into a diversified NATO/allied procurement pipeline.

**FY2026 and Q4 2026 results (anticipated March 2027).** The full-year print is the decisive data point for the investment thesis. Revenue conversion from defense ISR demand to booked and recognized contracts will be measured against ~~the trajectory implied by 2025 disclosures~~ ==the at-least-$390 million FY2026 target, with the pro forma $457 million backlog (including the Mistral and World View acquisitions closed in April 2026) as the supporting reference==. The Ondas Networks ~~segment~~ ==business (deconsolidated in January 2026 and now held outside the consolidated reporting perimeter)== will be scrutinized for cumulative deployment progress: by this point the AAR-coordinated industry initiative will have been in discussion for several years, and any continued delay in commercial network deployment — moving from field trials to revenue-generating subscription or capacity-based contracts with Class I railroads — will erode patience among longer-duration holders. Management's FY2027 outlook commentary will set the tone for the next re-rating window.

**Q1 2027 results (anticipated May 2027).** The year-over-year comparison will be against Q1 2026, ~~which itself should reflect some benefit from Israeli MoD demand acceleration~~ ==which printed $50.1 million of revenue, already exceeding the $50.7 million delivered for all of FY2025==. Investors will be calibrating whether the growth trajectory remains intact into the new fiscal year or whether 2026 represented peak defense-cycle tailwind. Any guidance for FY2027 organic growth — specifically the trajectory toward an operating breakeven timeline — will be the dominant narrative driver at this juncture.

## Consensus estimates and the growth equation

Given the sub-four-analyst coverage universe, published consensus carries wide error bars. ~~Based on the disclosed financial structure and the trajectory of Airobotics and American Robotics revenue contributions, the implied aggregate revenue envelope for FY2026 sits in the range of $25–35 million at the frozen snapshot, representing a material step-up from the low-double-digit millions that characterized the pre-Airobotics baseline.~~ ==Management's May 14, 2026 update set the FY2026 revenue target at no less than $390 million, with roughly $230 million of that envelope tied to acquisitions completed during the year; the comparison baseline is FY2025 revenue of $50.7 million and FY2022's $2.1 million pre-Airobotics level.== Operating losses are expected to remain substantial — ~~likely in the $20–30 million range~~ ==scaling with the much-enlarged revenue base and integration spend== inclusive of non-cash stock-based compensation, depreciation on acquisition-related intangibles, and ongoing R&D investment — as the company continues to fund platform scaling ahead of profitability.

| Period | Revenue Consensus (est.) | Implied YoY Growth | Operating Loss (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025 (actual) | ~~$18–22M~~ ==$50.7M== | — | ~$(22–28)M |
| FY2026 (guided) | ~~$25–35M~~ ==at least $390M (May 14, 2026 raise)== | ~~30–60%~~ ==~670%== | ~~$(18–26)M~~ ==materially larger, scaling with revenue and integration spend== |
| FY2027 (early view) | ~~$35–50M~~ ==(no published target)== | ~~30–50%~~ ==n/a== | ~~$(12–20)M~~ ==scenario-dependent== |

*Estimates derived from structural analysis; thin analyst bench means ranges should be treated as scenario bounds, not point estimates.*

The EPS metric is less useful here than cash consumption. With a fully diluted share count that has grown materially through ~~successive ATM offerings~~ ==successive ATM offerings and the January 2026 raise — from 93,173,191 shares at December 31, 2024 to 495,762,650 outstanding as of May 13, 2026==, per-share loss figures are heavily influenced by equity issuance pace. The more relevant operating metric is quarterly cash burn relative to balance-sheet cash, and by extension the implied quarters of runway ~~without additional dilution~~ ==against the $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments on the Q1 2026 balance sheet==.

## The metrics that matter, segment by segment

**Ondas Autonomous Systems.** The primary watch metrics are: (1) Airobotics Israeli MoD contract backlog as disclosed in quarterly filings or earnings call commentary — any disclosure of multi-year contract value is a significant positive signal; (2) American Robotics Scout System deployment count and number of paying commercial customers — oil/gas, rail, and mining inspection contracts are the near-term commercial pathway; (3) any ~~BVLOS regulatory advancement under the FAA reauthorization framework that broadens addressable markets for Part 107 autonomous operations~~ ==expansion of the existing FAA BVLOS waiver — which already permits flights over people and moving vehicles from a centralized remote operations center subject to waiver terms — into broader Part 107 authorizations==.

**Ondas Networks ==(deconsolidated January 2026)==.** The watch metrics are: (1) number of Class I railroad nodes or route-miles under active deployment versus pilot or negotiation stage; (2) any formal AAR program-of-record announcement that accelerates industry-wide adoption of the FullMAX platform; (3) revenue recognized from the rail ~~segment~~ ==business== each quarter, which has historically lagged the commercial pipeline narrative.

**Capital structure.** ~~ATM utilization pace disclosed in quarterly 8-K filings and the cash position disclosed in each balance-sheet snapshot. A drawdown rate exceeding $6–8 million per quarter would flag a dilution trajectory that pressures the per-share math materially at current market capitalizations.~~ ==Deployment pace of the $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments disclosed at March 31, 2026 — the live watch item is acquisition cadence and integration spend rather than near-term equity dilution, with the post-financing share count of roughly 496 million already setting the per-share denominator for any go-forward earnings.==

## Beat versus miss

A **beat** against current expectations requires at least two of: Airobotics quarterly revenue exceeding $6–8 million for two consecutive quarters; a new non-Israeli defense customer (DIU, NATO allied, US Army) generating recognizable revenue in the period; Ondas Networks transitioning at least one Class I railroad customer from field trial to commercial contract; or a ~~quarterly cash position improving sequentially through operating leverage rather than through new equity issuance~~ ==demonstrable narrowing of operating losses through the contribution of the April 2026 Mistral and World View acquisitions==.

A **miss** is most likely to manifest as: Israeli MoD revenue concentration risk crystallizing — either through contract timing delays or procurement budget shifts — without offsetting wins in the US or allied pipeline; continued Ondas Networks deployment slippage pushing commercial revenue recognition into future periods; or ~~an ATM drawdown pace that implies fewer than six quarters of runway without additional capital actions~~ ==FY2026 revenue tracking materially below the at-least-$390 million target, particularly if the acquisition-dependent ~$230 million slug fails to convert==.

## The bull and bear setup

The bull case rests on convergence. Three independent growth vectors — defense ISR drone demand, commercial automated inspection, and rail private wireless — do not need to fire simultaneously; they simply need to progress without simultaneous reversal. The Airobotics platform has a verifiable Israeli MoD customer base, a proven deployment record in Dubai, and a defense-export pathway into Western allied procurement that remains structurally underpenetrated. A single US government program-of-record announcement — or a disclosed contract with a NATO-member defense ministry — would represent a step-change in the revenue multiple the market assigns.

The bear case is ~~a dilution spiral with delayed revenue~~ ==a revenue ramp falling well short of the at-least-$390 million FY2026 target, with the dramatically expanded share count amplifying any per-share disappointment==. Ondas has funded its growth ~~entirely~~ through equity issuance since the ~~corporate parent formation in 2017~~ ==2018 reverse acquisition of Ondas Networks==. If defense ISR revenue conversion remains lumpy and back-end weighted, ~~the company will need to continue drawing on its ATM facility at a pace that structurally impairs per-share value creation~~ ==the share-count expansion from 93 million at year-end 2024 to roughly 496 million by mid-May 2026 will continue to weigh on per-share value creation even with $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments now on the balance sheet==. The concentration risk in Israeli-centric revenue is real: geopolitical or budgetary shifts in Israeli MoD procurement could clip the principal growth driver without the US commercial pipeline yet ready to absorb the shortfall.

The asymmetry as of May 2026 is that the downside is well-understood and priced into a de-rated valuation, while the upside — a single large US defense contract or a formal AAR deployment commitment from a Class I railroad — is binary and not yet priced. That is the setup into the next four quarterly prints.

chapters.title: Defense ISR scaling, commercial inspection ramp, rail private wireless, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## A Platform Built for the Inflection

By the close of fiscal 2025, Ondas Holdings had ~~spent eight years~~ ==spent seven years== assembling what chairman and chief executive Eric Brock described as a "full-stack autonomous systems and private wireless platform" — a configuration of assets that, viewed individually, each occupied a narrow niche but, viewed together, mapped onto three of the most structurally durable technology demand cycles of the decade: the global defense ISR drone surge, the commercial automated inspection ramp, and the long-deferred modernization of North American rail's mission-critical communications backbone. The question entering 2026 was no longer whether those cycles were real. It was whether Ondas, operating from a still-modest revenue base and ~~reliant on equity capital to fund its burn~~ ==now sitting on roughly $1.48 billion of cash, restricted cash and short-term investments after a January 2026 financing==, could convert structural positioning into durable, repeatable contract revenue ~~before its capital runway required further dilution~~ ==at the pace implied by the at-least-$390 million FY2026 revenue target management set in May 2026==.

The answer would be written across four distinct arenas.

## Defense ISR: Airobotics and the Western Procurement Wave

The January 2023 acquisition of Airobotics transformed Ondas Autonomous Systems from a commercially oriented inspection-drone platform into a credentialed defense ISR operator with an active engagement inside the Israeli Ministry of Defense and the Iron Dome border-security apparatus. That repositioning proved better-timed than management could have anticipated. The October 2023 outbreak of conflict in Gaza accelerated Israeli procurement of autonomous border-surveillance and ISR capability, and Airobotics' Optimus System — an urban automated drone-in-a-box platform with established Israeli homeland-security deployments — was already in the procurement conversation.

Through 2024 and into 2025, Israeli MoD disclosures and Ondas earnings-call commentary described an expanding engagement around persistent perimeter surveillance and ISR relay applications, integrating with broader Israeli air-defense architecture. The revenue contribution, while growing, remained concentrated and lumpy, reflecting the contract-by-contract cadence of sovereign defense procurement rather than subscription-style commercial revenue. The strategic importance, however, was amplifying: Israel's documented willingness to deploy autonomous drone infrastructure at scale provided Airobotics with operational proof points that Western allied procurement offices — across NATO, the Indo-Pacific theatre, and the Gulf — increasingly treated as qualifying credentials rather than mere marketing references.

The Ukraine conflict had already restructured Western allied thinking about drone ISR. The visible dominance of low-cost, high-volume autonomous platforms in the Donbas and the Ukrainian southern front made legacy procurement timelines politically untenable. Defense ministries from Warsaw to Canberra were compressing evaluation cycles and expanding small-UAS and autonomous-system budget lines. Ondas positioned Airobotics — and, where applicable, the American Robotics Scout System — as the infrastructure-grade, automated-logistics answer to that demand: not expendable tactical munitions but persistent, reusable ISR nodes capable of operating without human pilots in the loop. That distinction mattered for procurement offices seeking platforms that could survive repeated operational cycles rather than being consumed on first use.

The competitive landscape remained formidable. AeroVironment ([NASDAQ: AVAV](https://www.avinc.com/investors)) had revenue at scale, established DoD procurement relationships, and a deep portfolio of small-UAS and tactical missile systems. Shield AI, Anduril, and Skydio — all private-capital backed — were deploying at speed across different autonomous-platform categories. Ondas' competitive differentiation rested on the automated-logistics dock infrastructure (the Optimus and Scout dock-and-recharge stations that enable BVLOS operations without ground crews), the Israeli operational credentialing, and the FullMAX private wireless network that could, in principle, provide the communications backbone for drone swarms operating in contested or RF-congested environments.

## American Robotics: The Commercial Inspection Ramp

While Airobotics drove the defense ISR narrative, American Robotics — acquired in August 2021 and headquartered in Marlborough, Massachusetts — continued the slower, sturdier build of the commercial automated inspection market. The Scout System had distinguished itself by being the first drone platform to receive FAA Part 107 BVLOS waivers for fully automated operations, a regulatory milestone that founder Reese Mozer and his team had pursued methodically before the Ondas acquisition. That waiver portfolio remained a structural competitive advantage through 2025: prospective customers in oil and gas, mining, utility, and rail inspection could deploy Scout without on-site remote pilots, a cost-structure advantage that conventional drone-services firms could not replicate.

The commercial scaling trajectory through 2024-2025 showed meaningful expansion in deployed units and customer engagement, with rail inspection — where American Robotics had natural alignment with Ondas Networks' rail customer base — emerging as a priority vertical.
